en: *Shoulengyan Jing Jijie Xunwen Ji*, Scroll One,
composed by the Śramaṇa Renyue of Wuxing.
I take refuge in the Tathāgatagarbha, The revealed and secret Sūtra, And the Teacher, Śākyamuni.

To those who know all within the dust-motes of lands—Mañjuśrī, Ānanda, and the rest of the Bodhisattvas and noble Sangha—I pray that you, through your unconditioned compassion, provide witness and protection.
In the past, various Dharma masters have commented upon the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama*; I have now compiled these [teachings] and transmit them to those who uphold this sutra.
The commentary is not yet detailed, and its circulation remains limited; thus, I shall now recount it once more to assist those who are still ignorant.
May we, like Avalokiteśvara, purify our hearing and attain perfect enlightenment.

Having already explained the title of the scripture as in a separate fascicle, I shall now interpret the text. The words and phrases are divided into three parts: first, the introductory section; second, [the main body]; third, [the concluding section]. (Note: The second and third parts are implied by the structure.)

The *Zhengzongfen* (Main Section), the *Sanliutongfen* (Section on the Propagation of the Teaching). Initially, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, Master Dao’an established this threefold division to classify and explain various scriptures.
Later, when Master Xuanzang translated the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* during the Tang dynasty, the Western Indian Bodhisattva Sthiramati classified the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* into three parts:
first, the "Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching"; second, the "Section on What is Taught in the Holy Teachings"; and third, the "Section on the Basis."

The section on "Instruction for Practice" (Jiaofengxingfen) shares the same meaning as the sections on the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination (Xuzhengliutong), though the phrasing differs;

thus, one knows that Master An’s arrangement is in profound accord with the teachings of Bandhuprabha. In this scripture, the portion from "Thus have I heard" up to "Exhorting Ānanda and Mādrī-devī to return to the Buddha's presence" constitutes the Introductory Section (Xufen).
From "Ānanda sees the Buddha" up to the ninth fascicle [is the Main Body], while the remainder is the Dissemination Section (Liutongfen).
The "Speaker" refers to Māra, who speaks as the Main Body (zhengzongfen). Immediately following, the Tathāgata, about to descend from the Dharma-seat, provides the Dissemination Section (liutongfen).
Within the Introductory Section (xufen), it is further divided into two parts: first, from "Thus have I heard" up to Mañjuśrī, which constitutes the upper part.
The first part is the *Saddharmapratyayana-nidāna* (Preface of Authentic Faith); the second, from "At that time, King Prasenajit" onwards, is the *Utpatti-nidāna* (Preface of Origination).
These two are also termed the "General Preface" and the "Specific Preface. The General Preface applies across all teachings, while the Specific Preface pertains to a single sūtra.

Regarding the first, the Preface of Authentic Faith, the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is intended to prevent doubt in those who hear it. As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Final Chapter, states: "When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa..."
Ānanda asked the Buddha: "After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, what words should be placed at the beginning of all the sūtras when the Dharma-piṭaka is compiled?

The Buddha said: "One should place these words: 'Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a place, together with the fourfold assembly, and there he spoke this sūtra.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The sūtras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time all begin by citing the phrase 'Thus' (*evam*). This is the standard.
The preface to the *Xingfu shijing* (Preface to the Scripture on the Arising of Blessings) consists of six points: first, the Dharma heard; second, the person who hears;
third, the time of the teaching; fourth, the master who bestows the transformation; fifth, the place where the Dharma is expounded; and sixth, the assembly of those who hear together.
Zizhong combines these six matters into two gates: first, the time and place of the scripture’s delivery; second, the leading of the assembly to hear it together. As for...
Changshui likewise followed this usage, yet he now maintains that combining the preceding five matters into a single section is too brief in meaning;

therefore, he judges them according to their respective divisions into three phrases: first, the time of transmitting the Dharma; second, the place where the Buddha appeared; and third, the assembly of those who heard it together.
Regarding the first, the time of transmitting the Dharma, this refers to "Thus have I heard at one time. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also treats these six characters in this manner.
I shall now compose a chapter to explain this, following the precedent of previous works. To examine its origins:
prior to the Jin and Wei dynasties, most translated scriptures often began with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) or "I have heard thus.

It was not until the Later Qin, when Kumārajīva translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, that the formula "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) became established as the standard convention. The annotation "Gushan" refers to the residence of Master Yuan.

Regarding the phrase "downward toward the limit of reality" (*tattvānta*), Changshui and others all refer to the location by the name of the person; this is fully explained in the titles of their commentaries and sub-commentaries.

As for "the Dharma that has been transmitted," it refers to the Buddha’s teachings—both the expressive words (*vyañjana*) and the expressed meaning (*artha*)—as transmitted by the compilers of the canon.

Because the expressive texts do not differ from the Buddha's own words, it is said [they are] "like" them; because the expressed principles are nothing other than the truth, it is said [they are] "real."
Furthermore, because the text accords with the principle, it is said to be "according to the principle" (*yūrta*); because the principle accords with the text, it is said to be "thus.

Since this principle permeates the four teachings, the characteristics of such dharmas—whether partial or complete—are as distinguished in detail in the various *sūtra* commentaries of Tiantai. Here, we exclude the partial and take the complete;
the sole *tathāgatagarbha-citta* (the mind of the Tathāgata-store) is the dharma-body of this sūtra, and its category belongs to the "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*).
The lecturer understands this fully. As for those capable of transmitting [the teachings], Ānanda speaks for himself. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"In the Buddha-dharma, it is said that all phenomena are empty and that there is no self (*ātman*). Why, then, does the beginning of the Buddhist sūtras state, 'Thus have I heard'? It answers:
"Although the disciples of the Buddha know there is no self, they speak of a 'self' in accordance with worldly convention; it is not a real self."

Regarding "hearing": when the faculty of the ear is unimpaired, the sound reaches the range of audibility, and one applies the attention (*manasikāra*) with the desire to hear, then through the harmony of the sense organ, the object, and the mind, hearing is attained.
According to the *Fourfold Teachings* (Sijiao yi), Mount Gushan explains four types of "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*):
1. "I" and "I" hear; hearing is heard. 2. "I" and "non-I" hear; hearing is not heard. 3. "Non-I" and "I" do not hear; hearing is heard. 4. Neither "I" nor "non-I"; neither hearing nor non-hearing.
Regarding "hearing" and "not hearing," the first three instances of "I have heard" refer to the meaning of the expedient means (*upāya*) heard in the past;

the final instance of "I have heard" refers to the present primary intent. Because those of recent learning receive only a superficial impression and because extensive detail would be cumbersome, this collected commentary dissolves the text and presents it with brevity.
Regarding the phrase "the time of meeting the opportunity and realizing the principle," the *Gushan Guying Chao* states: "Meeting" means to come together. This refers to...
Now, because the teaching of the *Śūraṅgama* accords with the capacities of beings in the present and future, it is said to "accord with the capacity" (*jī*).
Because it accords with the eternally abiding true mind, it is said to "accord with the principle" (*lǐ*). The unification of capacity and principle is precisely what is intended here.
Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard from the Buddha," this is an explanation based on the phenomenal aspect (*shìxiàng*). The *Tōnghuì Shēngxìn Chāo* states that "such as these" refers to...
Ānanda accepted [the instruction]. Kāśyapa raised the words of the inquiry; to be able to raise them means to speak by means of the Dharma previously heard—this refers to the title of the sutra.
How could there not be phrases, pauses, and several characters? Yet, regarding the meaning of the response, he instead grasped it in its entirety and did not transcribe the verbose details;
therefore, it says "Thus" (*evam*). This is like people today who, when discussing something, acknowledge what preceded.
People’s intention is that it is the same in this regard; thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Thus have I heard" means to manifest in general what has already been heard, being the words of the transmitter of the Buddha’s teachings, signifying: "I have previously heard such matters.

Regarding the time when the teaching was spoken, "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers generally to the conclusion of the sutra. For example, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha says: "In the past, at one time, I was at the Ganges..."
The *Anhui shu* (Commentary by Anhui) further states: "At one time I was in the kingdom of Kāśī," and so forth; the details are the same [as in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*].

Regarding the two Buddhas being in the lower realm and the place where they inspired the Buddha, the inclusion of the Sanskrit terms and so on is also from the *Zhenshi ji shu* (Commentary on the *Tattvārtha*).

Although the scriptural texts are separated, the interpreters do not differ; thus, no specific headings are provided, and all other instances follow this pattern. The full text of that section is contained in the *Fodi lun* (Buddhabhūmi-śāstra), fascicle lower.

It is said that one who possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), being free from the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
is able to awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects for oneself and is also able to awaken all sentient beings—

like awakening from a dream or like the blooming of a lotus— and is therefore called a Buddha. One should know that "all-knowledge" regarding "all phenomena" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The "object of wisdom" refers to the object of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Regarding the "aspects of all aspects":

the object of conventional truth wisdom is so called because, by illuminating the ultimate truth, it is free from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and is able to awaken oneself; and because, by illuminating the conventional truth, it is free from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and is able to awaken all sentient beings.
The metaphors "like awakening from sleep and dream" and "like the blooming of a lotus flower" collectively illustrate the meaning of the two types of wisdom’s realization and comprehension.

Furthermore, the metaphor of awakening from a dream illustrates that true wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) cannot be apprehended as a single entity; the metaphor of a flower blooming illustrates that conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) perceives all various phenomena.
Regarding the terms "being present" (*zài*) and "abiding" (*zhù*), some say that "being present" refers to a temporary stay, while "abiding" refers to a long-term residence.

However, following the various commentaries of the Tiantai school, "being present" is itself "abiding. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the four modes of physical deportment are all termed "abiding. Furthermore, it is also... [text continues].
Because he causes his disciples to enter various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) by terrifying the demonic armies, he abides therein.

Regarding the Buddha’s internal abiding in *Śūraṅgama*, the treatise clarifies four kinds of abiding: first, the "abiding of heaven" (*devasthāna*), which refers to generosity, ethical discipline, and a virtuous mind;
second, the "abiding of Brahmā" (*brahmavihāra*), which refers to the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and even the perception of foulness.
The "Dwelling of the Celestial Cause" refers to the three samādhis: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

The "Dwelling of the Four Buddhas" refers to the power of the hundred and eight samādhis such as Śūraṅgama, and the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates for saving beings, including the [four] fearlessnesses.

Although the Buddha dwells in meditative concentration, he manifests in accordance with human ways; his four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—are perfectly complete. This arises from himself.

Because the *saṃbhogakāya* internally accords with the profound nature of reality (*dharmatā*) while externally responding to the multitudes of beings, it is said to be "able to establish great benefit.

Regarding the term "traces abiding" (*jizhu*): "traces" is a name given in contrast to the "original" (*ben*). Speaking in terms of lands, the original dwells in the Land of Tranquil Light (*jiguang*), while the traces reside in the Sahā world.
This is like the example from Central India where the capital city of the kingdom of Kośala is referred to by its title; this was verified by Xie Li.
The *Shinzō* (True Commentary) states: "In order to distinguish it from the Southern Kośala country, the name of the kingdom is omitted and the designation of the city is used.

Regarding "wealth" (*hōzai*): Cai [Yuan]’s commentary on the *Huàqīng jīng* says, "Wealth (*huò*) means transformation; because it is an object that undergoes change and reversal, the character contains the radical for 'transformation' (*huà*).

Regarding "the realm of desire" (*yùjìng*): this refers to the objects of the five sensory dusts (*pañca-viṣaya*), which give rise to the mind of necessity and desire in people. "Many... [text continues].
Regarding "Śrāvastī," the Tripitaka Master Yijing translated it as "Renowned Name" (Mingcheng), which captures only one aspect of its meaning.

"One capable of liberation" refers to a renunciant who has severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Regarding "Jetavana," Changshui states that the full name is Jetā, which means "Victorious in Battle"—this is the name of the Prince;
"vana" means "grove. However, it is incorrect to claim that *vana* itself means "grove."
According to both the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) and Master Ying’s *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings), it is stated that "Ji-huan" (祇洹) is a corruption;

the correct term is "Shidi" (逝多), which translates as "Śyāma. If one refers to it as a "grove," the Sanskrit term is "vana. Thus, we know that the character "Huan" (桓) is no different from "Huan" (洹).
Regarding "Jetavana" (須達市園): its full name is Sudatta, which is translated as "Givaka" (給孤獨) or "Good Giver" (善施). "Shi" (市) means to purchase.

The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that when the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada heard of the Buddha’s meritorious virtues, he conceived a profound sense of reverence and wished to construct a vihāra to invite the Buddha to descend there.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra to survey the site; [he found] only Prince Jeta’s [garden].

The site was vast and the grounds were clear and pleasant; [Śāriputra] went there to see the Prince and informed him of his intentions in full detail. The Prince spoke in jest, saying, "If gold were spread everywhere, then it could be sold.
When Sudatta heard this, his heart felt as if suddenly cleared of clouds. He immediately brought out the gold from his treasury and, following the Prince's words, spread it across the ground.

Where there was a small area not yet covered, the Prince requested that it be left as it was and offered it to the Buddha, saying, "This is truly a fertile field where one ought to plant the seeds of merit. Thereupon, he constructed [a monastery] upon that open space.
When the vihāra was being erected, the World-Honored One went there and addressed Ānanda, saying: "The site was well-purchased by Sudatta, and the grove-trees were donated by Jeta;
as these two have joined their hearts in reverence for this meritorious work, from this day forward this place should be called the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."
The assembly of those who heard together consists of two groups: first, the assembly of *śrāvakas*, and second, the assembly of *pratyekabuddhas*.

The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fahua lun) clarifies that the *śrāvakas* are listed first to demonstrate that they personally heard [the teaching] and will not later slander it, and furthermore, to include those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.

It continues by stating that this is also "to cause the bodhisattvas to show respect. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Di lun) is largely the same; one should know that both treatises maintain that there are five natures (*pañca-gotra*).

The various schools all claim that those of indeterminate nature merely turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; however, this sutra demonstrates that those of determinate nature all attain the One Vehicle.
By contrast, it is proven that the assertions of those schools were merely provisional teachings.

First, regarding the assembly of śrāvakas, there are three parts: first, the designation of their category. The phrase "with a great assembly of bhikṣus" indicates that they were together with [the Buddha].
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains "commonality" (*sādhāraṇa*) by means of seven meanings: namely, one place, one time, one mind, one precept, one view, one path, and one liberation.
It is called "common" because Ānanda shares these seven meanings with the assembly. As for the Sanskrit term *mahat*, this is translated here as "Great.
Alternatively, it is said to mean "much" or "superior," because he is honored by great beings such as the Heavenly Kings. Thus, he is "Great."
Furthermore, they number as many as one thousand two hundred and fifty; thus, they are "many. They are "victorious" because they can defeat the ninety-six types of heterodox disputants.
[Note: The term *bhikṣu* (monk) contains three meanings: because he lives a pure life, he is called a "beggar" (*yācaka*);

because he can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), he is called a "destroyer of evil" (*pāpavināśaka*). From the time of shaving the hair until the moment of receiving the precepts, the Māra says: "This person will certainly..."
Because one attains *nirvāṇa*, one is called "Terrifier of Māras. From these three causes, the three names on the level of fruition are established;

these correspond to the three meanings of an *arhat* mentioned below: from the cause of being a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), the fruit of being "Worthy of Offerings" (*dakṣiṇīya*) is achieved; from the cause of destroying evil, the fruit of being a "Slayer of Thieves" (*vadhaka*) is achieved;
and from the cause of terrifying Māra, the fruit of "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*) is achieved. A group of four or more individuals is termed a "community" (*saṃgha*) in the Sanskrit sense.
Regarding the term *saṃgha*, this refers to a harmonious assembly; since the matter of reciting the precepts can be accomplished by four people, it may be understood that there are many more.
As for the three Kāśyapas: first, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; second, Gayā-Kāśyapa; and third, Nadī-Kāśyapa, as detailed in the commentary to the fifth fascicle.
The elder brother had five hundred disciples, while each of the two younger brothers had two hundred.
Five hundred and one thousand people. ▲ Those who previously served the fire are as described in this sutra:

"All the Kāśyapas, together with the Brahmins, diligently applied their minds and exhausted their bodies to serve the fire and venerate water, seeking those who transcend birth and death. This refers to them.

▲ Regarding the turning away from heterodoxy and entering into the correct path, the *Fahua shuji* (Record of the Lotus Sutra Commentary) explains in detail how the Tathāgata performed ten kinds of supernatural transformations to convert the non-Buddhists.
Lupiṇḍika and his disciples all submitted and attained the fruit of *śrāmaṇya*; they took their ritual implements and cast them into the water, where they drifted downstream.
When the two younger brothers and five hundred disciples saw this, they also all returned to the Buddha, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "The Way within the inner darkness," it refers to the teaching after the provisional was opened; the subsequent passage praising his virtues is complete. According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*... [end of fragment].
In that sūtra, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa asks the Buddha how one may attain vastness and become a refuge for the multitude, to which the Buddha replies in the chapter on the "Four Reliances.
The text states: "There are four kinds of persons who can protect the True Dharma and serve as a reliance for the world;
these are the persons of the four fruits. It further says: "The person of the fourth fruit is named Arhat; they have severed all afflictions."
Abiding in the tenth stage, one attains the wisdom of mastery and is able to manifest all manner of forms and images according to the inclinations of beings.
Now, Master Gu Shan’s intention is that the entire great assembly consists of those who have taken the ten stages as their root while manifesting the four fruits as their traces;

this is spoken from the perspective of the majority. Among them, there must certainly be those who have been appropriately granted the opening of the provisional [teachings], such as those who have entered the first abode.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, during the three successive turnings of the wheel, those who received their predictions of enlightenment—how could there not have been such people?
The second section, "The Two Disciples," praises their virtues. Regarding the annotation on "opening the provisional and revealing the trace":

as it is said, "Opening the gate of expedient means to reveal the true aspect" and "decisively resolving that the Śrāvaka Dharma is the king of all sūtras"—this is the passage concerning the opening of the provisional. Furthermore...
It is said that because they know the multitude delights in inferior teachings and fears great wisdom, the Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
this is the passage concerning their revealed origins. "Born from the Buddha’s mouth" refers to hearing the teaching of the expressive sounds (*śabda*).

"Born through transformation from the Dharma" refers to awakening to the true principle of the expressed reality (*artha*). Because of these teachings and principles, there is the Dharmakāya and the life of wisdom.

Thereupon, one gives rise to the stage of the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), which is a partial realization of truth (*satyābhisamaya*). Because one can manifest the eight phases of a Buddha’s life within the hundred realms to benefit sentient beings, it is said that "one has attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
"Capable of succeeding to the lineage of the Buddhas" explains the meaning of "abiding" (*vihāra*).

The "secret treasury of the three virtues" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), Prajñā, and Liberation; these are called the secret treasury. "Abiding and maintaining" explains the meaning of "sustaining" (*dhṛti*). It is like the eighty thousand [precepts].
The four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates are the total retention (*saṃgraha*) of wholesome dharmas. Regarding the "twenty-five existences" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*):

this refers to the four continents, the four evil destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm, as well as the Brahma heavens, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the five non-returners (*anāgāmin*), and so forth.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that by means of the twenty-five kingly samādhis, one destroys the twenty-five existences; first, one employs the stainless [samādhi].

Regarding the statement that "the Samādhi of Breaking through the Hell of Darkness up to the Realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is called the King of Samādhis," the wise explain that while emptiness and the provisional have not yet attained the status of king,
it is because the Middle Way harmonizes and perfects the truth that it is entitled to be called the King. As for the passage in the sutra stating,
"one who can achieve majestic deportment within the lands," this refers to transcending all realms of existence beforehand, thereby ascending to harmonize with the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The fundamental, wondrous, enlightened mind now manifests as dignified deportment; this refers to the subsequent merging with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions.
*Note:* Regarding "possessing dignity" (*yǒuwēi*), the *Zuǒchuán* states: "To possess dignity such that one is feared is called *wēi*;

to possess deportment such that one may be emulated is called *yí*. It further states: "When a ruler possesses the dignity and deportment of a ruler, his ministers will both fear and love him. Then...
Because they receive this [protection], they are able to possess their states and enjoy long-lasting renown;
their ministers possess the dignified bearing of ministers, and their subordinates revere and love them, thus enabling them to maintain their offices and preserve their clans and households.

Their good reputation brings forth further renown, and their dignified bearing inspires those who have left the household life to revere and emulate them, thereby enabling them to follow the Buddha’s wheel-turning and excellently sustain his legacy.
Regarding the entrustment and so forth: the subsequent citation of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* serves to reveal the inconceivable function [of this samādhi]. The Wise One (Zhi-zhe) said:

"Śrāvakas cannot manifest the four dignified postures (*iryāpatha*) while in meditative absorption; for example, Kāśyapa remained in absorption until the appearance of Maitreya before he could manifest transformations.
Because inconceivable samādhi possesses both essence and function, it is able to manifest various postures without arising from concentration."
The *śūrpa* lute emits its melodies in accordance with the person playing it. Regarding the principle that the Dharma has the meaning of crushing and grinding away afflictions (*kleśa*):

because the Buddha’s teaching enters the minds of others and, furthermore, it is through the practice of the Dharma that one can destroy delusions, the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) explains that the teaching is the "turner" (*pravartaka*) and the practice is the "turned" (*vartya*);
only when the subject and object unite does one obtain the name of a "wheel" (*cakra*). Regarding the vision of the Buddha from beginning to end: the beginning...

From the Deer Park to the Crane Forest, these accounts are likewise spoken by way of generalization. For instance, if Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had entered parinirvāṇa prior to the Buddha, they would not have reached the final nirvana;
yet the present sutra states that he offered his final instructions, which already carries the sense of a bequest, as cited in the following text.
... [The passage continues: "Even unto the arrival of Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and others," where the *Guxiang* commentary notes: "At that time, Kāśyapa..."
The Venerable Śāriputra entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) on Vulture Peak Mountain and did not emerge until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
Ānanda remained outside the Śāla grove, ensnared by Māra, and did not arrive until the Buddha was on the verge of passing away. Regarding the *Vinaya*, "vinaya" means "to discipline";

as the *Guxiang* (Echoing Valley) commentary states, it is a "scale" (*quan*) for weighing the gravity of offenses, determining what constitutes a transgression and what does not. By following its precepts, one transcends birth and death.
The *Śāsanottara-sūtra* states: "By relying on this precept, one attains all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.

This is also explained in the section on the "Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body" (*Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*) within Avalokiteśvara’s discourse on the "Perfect Penetration" (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*). Now, according to the intent of this section, the primary concern is for those in the future age;

this refers precisely to the meaning of the "Dharma entrusted at the end" mentioned previously. Furthermore, Ānanda said: "Although I have not yet attained liberation, I pray that you will deliver those of the future."
Having thus identified all the sentient beings throughout the kalpas, Ānanda, their names are listed below in three sections.
[Note: Some are ranked according to their seniority in years of ordination (*varṣāgra*), as in the case of Kauṇḍinya mentioned in the following text, who said:
"In the Deer Park and at the Cock’s Garden, I witnessed the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of enlightenment and his Buddha-voice."
"Wuming Sidi" (Awakening to the Four Truths) refers to the name for the year-end sacrifice. The *Fengsu tong* states: "In the Xia dynasty it was called Jiaping;
in the Yin, Qingji; in the Zhou, Dajiao; and in the Han, La. "La" means "hunting"; one hunts for birds and beasts to sacrifice to the ancestors.
Others say that "La" means "to join," as it is the junction between the new and the old. Therefore, within the sutras and vinayas, it is referred to as the "Seventh [Month]."

Regarding the matter of "returning to eat until full," the *Guhya-ruta* (Valley Echo) quotes the *Āgama*, stating that it refers to those who have attained the three fruits.

Having left the household life, he fell away from his discipline (*śīla*) but did not lose the path shared with worldly people. People raised slanderous speech, saying, "He possesses no noble qualities (*āryadharma*).

The Buddha said, "He wishes to be satiated and has given rise to weariness; before long he shall return and again seek to go forth. The bhikṣus did not ordain him, but the Buddha immediately ordained him, and he attained the four fruits of the spiritual life.
Ānanda asked, "Venerable One, was this one who had fallen away from training (*śaikṣa*), or one who had fallen away from beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*)? He replied, "A trainee (*śaikṣa*)."
This refers to a person liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) who falls back; it describes the act of becoming a person of the first fruit (srotāpanna) within the body of that very first fruit.
Regarding the statement that "a person of the first fruit is born into a family of sheep-slaughterers," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

A person of the first fruit was born into a butcher's household and was approaching adulthood when he refused to kill living beings. His parents placed him together with a knife and a sheep inside a room and spoke to him, saying: [text continues]
"If you do not kill the sheep and do not force your son out, but instead commit suicide with a blade, you shall immediately be reborn in the heavens.
▲ Regarding this, the people of the world, following the Vinaya, say that one who brings about misfortune for others commits the offense of "touching" (the *mānusa-sparśana-śīla*). Zizhong says:
"According to the Vinaya, there is no offense if it is unintentional; however, because one should not enter a brothel alone, such an act constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."

Luo Zhenji said: "According to the sūtras, if one personally touches [a woman] with lustful intent, it destroys the essence of the precepts; this is called a 'near-preparatory act' (*upakrama*) within the category of non-precepts.

It constitutes a grave offense of *sthūlātyaya*. Although Ānanda was without lustful intent and was coerced by her, he still bears the name of an offense, yet lacks the actual substance of an offense.
If one claims that he committed the offense of touching and thus incurred a *duṣkṛta* (minor transgression), this does not fully capture the principle."

As for the claim that the offenses of *kuò* (negligence) and *yùn* (obstruction) are both inherently invalid, and the assertion that *yùn* cannot possibly explain away a text intended for destruction—Jiè argues that while *stūlāntika* has a name but lacks a substantial essence, I shall pose this question to him:
Does the Sūtra state that one "intends to destroy" because one desires to destroy, or because one does not desire to destroy?
If it is because one desires to destroy, why is there no substantial essence to the offense? If it is because one does not desire to destroy, why [is it still called such]?
To claim that this constitutes a transgression would mean that both [the original text and the correction] are incorrect, serving only to increase the confusion of later students.
Regarding the mother of the woman [Āmrapālī], her name was Mātaṅgī; "Mātaṅgī" is a transliteration of the Sanskrit *mā-taṅ-gī*.
According to the Wu edition, it states that Mātanga is of the Caṇḍāla caste, and thus this woman is also called a Caṇḍāla woman. Furthermore, it is said that at times there were people on the road...
While traveling, his carriage broke down, so he repaired it; thus he was named Mātaṅga. Gu Shan (孤山) says that according to what is stated there, this is a clan name for artisans (*śilpin*).

Now, based on the *Madhyama Āgama*, which explains the four castes—namely, Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Gṛhapati, and Śūdra—it is verified that Mātaṅga is indeed a caste name for artisans. Furthermore, Master Ying says, "Mā... [text breaks off].
*Taṅga* (fully transcribed as *Ātuda-maṭaṅgī-cāṇḍālī*) is the general name for a *maṭaṅgī*, while *ātudā* is a specific name for such a woman.
This woman was of low birth and made her living by constantly sweeping the marketplaces to provide herself with food and clothing.

Regarding the fact that the meaning of the translation by Changshui has not been seen: it appears that Master Xuán, seeing that the *Dengqie jing* (Sūtra of the Woman Dengqie) states this woman was formerly a Brahmin girl named Benxing, took that former name to translate her present-day identity.

Furthermore, others have translated it as "Defiled Wind," claiming that because men and women did not marry according to ritual propriety, they defiled the wind of the Five Constant Virtues; this too—
It is not so. As for the desire to refute the substance (*tǐ*) maintained by Ānanda, it is because one wishes to explain the "will" (*yù*).
This "substance" refers to the unmanifest substance (*avijñapti-tattva*) of the precept against sexual misconduct; the term "blemish" (*cī*)—as the *Shuowén* states—is a disease.
Second, "the Tathāgata extends his saving grace. ▲ "The Tathāgata who knows him" means knowing and illuminating;

this is because with the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is eternally illuminating while remaining in quiescence. ▲ "Fearless radiance" is for the sake of causing Ānanda to obtain fearless radiance;
that is, it is for the purpose of enabling Ānanda to attain fearlessness. ▲ Regarding "sitting in the full lotus posture," the *Śabdavidyā* (Treatise on Phonology) states:
He sits with his two feet crossed in the full lotus posture, his thighs joined like the coils of a dragon. [The note states: "The crown of the head represents the Dharma-body;
because the crown possesses the mark of the invisible summit, it symbolizes that the ultimate truth is unsurpassed and is not visible to those on lower stages."
▲ Regarding the light symbolizing the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body): there are two types of retribution—first, self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), and second, other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*).
The light now emitted is the aspect of other-enjoyment, while the body it symbolizes is the essence of self-enjoyment.

As the subsequent text states, "the light issues from the crown of the head," this means that wisdom arises from principle. ▲ Regarding the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*) symbolizing the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body): however...

Śākyamuni is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); furthermore, the term "manifestation" (*biao*) indicates that the application of this response is not singular. Is it not said that within one transformation there is yet another transformation? Question:
What does the production of thousand-petaled precious lotuses from within the light signify? Answer: The lotus signifies the Real (*shi*), while the flower signifies the Expedient (*quan*).
Since the response-body arises through its functions without departing from the two wisdoms of the Expedient and the Real, it is for this reason that the Transformation Buddha...
He sat cross-legged therein. "Universally illuminating the hundred realms" means that the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones—the ten realms—mutually contain one another.
"Subduing evil and gathering good" refers to subduing the evil of Dhanakara and gathering the goodness of Ānanda.

[The text] returns to the summary by Mañjuśrī. Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that says, "He went to protect [them] with mantras to promote merit," it means that Mañjuśrī secretly taught the subtle method for resolving heterodoxy;
thus, Ānanda did not hear it explicitly, but only received its protection in a hidden manner. Therefore, the seventh fascicle states:
"Although he has received the power of the Tathāgata’s *Buddhottama-dhāraṇī* through its hidden influence, he has not yet heard it personally. This is according to the *Tengqie jing*.
However, the World-Honored One himself spoke a mantra to counter that art of seduction. The sutra says:
"At that time, the Tathāgata, observing with his pure divine eye that Ānanda was being deluded and disturbed by that woman, spoke the following mantra for her protection:
Sittide (1), Ajude (2), Anide (3). Having spoken this mantra, he then said:"
"I declare that by means of this mantra, I shall bring peace and security to all sentient beings who are terrified, and I likewise desire to benefit and pacify those who suffer from affliction.
If there are sentient beings who have no place of refuge, I shall act as their true refuge.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse: "The pool of precepts is cool, pure, and stainless; it can bathe sentient beings of the fever of afflictions."

For those who possess wisdom, the dark obstructions of ignorance in this pool are forever extinguished; therefore, the sages and saints of the three periods of time all honor it with their heads bowed and praise it in unison.
"If I truly bathe in this stream, I shall cause my attendant to return quickly.
At that time, by the power of the Buddha and the power of his own roots of goodness, Ānanda found that the *caṇḍāla*’s incantations were powerless to affect him.
He immediately left his residence and returned to the Jeta Grove. One should know that the three secrets of the Sage respond to the capacities of beings;

since there are differences in what is seen and heard, one must not seek to interrogate him with ordinary sentiments. Guishan asked: "If he did not violate the precepts, why was it necessary for [the Buddha] to go and protect him? He replied:
"Because he was constrained by a spell, he lingered in the chamber of lust and could not leave of his own accord. Thus, in the passage below, Ānanda himself...
The preface states: "Having been constrained by the malevolent arts of that Brahmā, although his mind was clear, his power was not free;

therefore, he had to go to protect [the Buddha]. This is also like Ānanda at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, who was overwhelmed by Māra and relied on Mañjuśrī’s recitation of spells to go and rescue him.
It was merely to resolve his distress, not because one suspects him of being identical to the evil one. The commentary below clarifies this, which is in the fourth fascicle.
It is said that Mātaṅgī’s lust-fire was suddenly extinguished and she attained the stage of Anāgāmin; this refers to her attaining the third fruit after the incantation.
When she was subsequently brought back to the Buddha’s presence and heard the sutra until the section where Mañjuśrī selects the most perfect means of penetration, she finally became an Arhat.
According to the *Mātaṅga Sūtra*, it is stated that at the time she heard the incantation, no benefit had yet been mentioned; she sought out Ānanda and went to the Buddha’s presence herself.
Furthermore, it was not until Mañjuśrī had escorted her back and she heard him preach the Dharma that she attained the path of Arhatship.
Thus, in both sūtras, it is through hearing the sūtra that one realizes the four fruits; the difference lies only in the varying capacities and perspectives of those receiving the teaching.

Now, I shall further cite the Wu edition to briefly clarify the manner in which Dharmottarā returned to the Buddha, so that you may understand the significant differences between this sūtra and that one.
The Sūtra says: At that time, after the night had passed, the woman bathed her body, put on fresh clean garments, placed a flower garland upon her head, and adorned herself with fragrant unguents.
Walking slowly and with composure, she headed toward Śrāvastī;
having reached the city gate, she stood waiting for Ānanda. When Ānanda entered the city at dawn to beg for food, the woman saw him coming and felt deep [devotion].
Following him with joy, she never left his side. Seeing this, the Venerable One felt profound shame and returned to the Jeta Grove, where he prostrated before the Buddha and said:
"O World-Honored One, a candāla woman has tormented and harassed me; I pray that the World-Honored One will grant her protection through your compassion.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Do not be distressed; I shall cause you to escape this peril. At that time...
The World-Honored One said to the woman, "Do you intend to take Ānanda as your husband?
The woman replied, "It is so," and so on, until the Buddha said, "If you wish to have Ānanda as your husband, you should leave the household life and learn his appearance and attire.

She replied, "Yes, I respectfully accept your venerable instruction. The Buddha said, "Welcome! and she immediately became a śramaṇī; her hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the dharma robes appeared upon her.

While she was in her body, he preached the Dharma to her, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her with what is known as the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven;

he explained that sensual desires are impure, a mass of manifold sufferings, with little flavor but many disadvantages, being like a moth that, out of delusion, throws itself into a fierce flame. When the bhikṣuṇī heard this teaching, her mind became disciplined.
The Buddha, knowing her thoughts, immediately expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for her at length.

At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and she attained the path of Arhatship while still seated upon her mat, and so forth. Question: In that sūtra, one attains the four fruits of the śrāvaka path by hearing the "Small" [Dharma];
why then does one also realize Arhatship by hearing the "Great" [Dharma] in this sūtra? Answer: That [Small Vehicle] is separated from the Great, whereas this [Great Vehicle] is perfect and complete.

The general meaning is as explained in the sixth fascicle. ▲ Note: The following section clarifies the matter of Dantā’s attainment of benefit, which encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate.
Regarding Ānanda being drawn by the hook of desire, the *Guxiang* (Valley Resonance) says: "Love draws a person just as a hook draws an object. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"First one uses the hook of desire to draw them in, and later causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. Here, it concerns Dantā’s hearing of this [Dharma].
"Master Dian’s realization of the eternal mind is called 'entering the Buddha-wisdom'; this is spoken from the perspective of actual practice.
As for those of great transformative power (*mahopāya*), they are Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who manifest provisional traces to guide and receive those with genuine capacity.

Regarding the various commentaries, beginning with Master Guangtao of Beiguan during the Wei dynasty, who divided the sutra into eight sections, down to Guishan’s creation of the two gates of "Explanation" and "Practice," all [are included].
When the Buddha told Ānanda, "You and I share the same vital breath," this was the definitive teaching for the lower realms.

Now, observing the *Longshui Fen* (Longshui Section) Sūtra, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is the collective name for *śamatha* and its like; conversely, *śamatha* and its like are the specific designations for the *Śūraṅgama*.
This initial expedient means is also the essential gateway to perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), just as [the practice of] the body is within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The son requested the Buddha to manifest the true *nirvāṇa*, and Cunda requested the Buddha to discourse on the eternal;
both are correct teachings and do not belong to the introductory chapter—this precedent is clear.
Second, from "Ānanda saw the Buddha" onwards, the main body of the teaching (*samyak-artha*) is divided into three parts: first, Ānanda’s request. ▲ [In the] Sūtra, he weeps with grief.
When tears flow without making a sound, it is called weeping (*ruditam*). [Note: "Simultaneously arousing the mind" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
You, who have always been fond of much learning, possess great wisdom after having aroused the Great Mind, yet your concentration (*samādhi*) is slight.

That statement was made in reference to manifesting the fundamental nature; however, according to this present sutra, we must discuss it in terms of its traces (*vyañjana*). How is this clarified? As follows:

Ānanda himself recounted that his initial aspiration was based on the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and so forth; however, these were merely views of arising and ceasing characteristic of the Hīnayāna.
When the World-Honored One examined the location of his mind and vision and found they could not be located, it was clearly proven that he lacked the perfect understanding of the Mahāyāna.
This is truly because the text here states, "I regret that since beginningless time [my mind] has been like something secretly containing its original intent."
Therefore, Gushan cited the *Fahua Wenzong* to explain its meaning. ▲ From "I, by virtue of... below, he correctly addresses the provisional traces (*jiji*) to clarify his present intent.

Furthermore, Gushan’s interpretation states that those who are "exclusively learned" are biased toward minor wisdom (*xiao-hui*), while those who have "not yet perfected the power of the Way" have not cultivated the Great Samādhi (*da-ding*).
However, how could the Lesser Vehicle (*xiǎochéng*) lack the principle and samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*?

Furthermore, because they lack the perfectly integrated Buddha-wisdom, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states: "Since the śrāvakas possess no power of wisdom, the Tathāgata has taught them the 'half-syllables' (the conventional teachings).

Now, as the Tathāgata manifests supernatural powers and expounds the dhāraṇī, all of which issue forth from the stability of principle, he causes Ānanda to realize the inadequacy of limited wisdom and to specifically request the Great Samādhi. [The passage] beginning with "The Sūtra, out of earnestness... [follows].

Because it concerns the dharmas practiced by those who have attained the fruit according to their causal stages, it says, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the realization of Bodhi," and so forth;
this should be understood as meaning that the attainment of Bodhi is ultimate awakening wisdom (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*" refers to the meditative practices cultivated from the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhya-prthagjana*) up through the provisional and ultimate teachings of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). The *Śūraṅgama-dhāraṇī* encompasses both the cause and the fruit.

Regarding the "Attainment of the Fruit" (*abhisamaya-phala*), which is currently at the stage of the cause, the causal and resultant aspects follow one another from beginning to end in a single continuity;
the detailed analysis of its modes of activity is as previously explained. [Note: The general meaning of this corresponds to the "Threefold Contemplation of One Mind.

Master Zongmi, in his *Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, establishes three distinct names for these: first, the "Contemplation of Quelling Phenomena to Clarify the Spirit"; second, the "Contemplation of Arising Illusions to Dissolve Defilements."

The concluding summary of the "Threefold Contemplation of the Spiritually Responsive Mind Beyond Reliance" states: "This is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the three marks of *nirvāṇa*;

its principles are identical to those of Tiantai’s Three Contemplations, yet its intent differs. What is the same? The dissolution of marks is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the arising of illusions is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*);

and being beyond reliance is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). What is different? This [text] clarifies the skillful means for a person to employ the mind, whereas that [Tiantai system]..."

In investigating the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, this [approach] mostly concerns the accomplishment of mental activity (*citta-carita*); therefore, it does not establish an object of contemplation (*ālambana*).
That [approach] mostly concerns the arising of understanding through meaning; thus, in contrast to the three truths (*tri-satya*) which are the objects of contemplation, I now raise an objection:

since you speak of "mental application as a skillful means" (*upāya*), how can you also say it is "accomplished through mental activity"? Even if it were accomplished through activity, why does the scripture suddenly command "one [should contemplate]?"

All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who rely on the power of illusion before awakening practice what is called the "thorough investigation of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
This refers to the Tiantai school’s application of the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) contemplation to examine phenomena and their principles;

yet they do not know there is the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness). They merely attain the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) and do not employ any other path—how could they ever exclusively investigate the [ultimate] nature?

Furthermore, in general, when clearly contemplating the Way, one must distinguish it by means of the objects of the Truths (*satya*). As stated in the *Śamatha* section of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Vajrasamādhi-sūtra*):
"One takes stillness as the practice by means of the pure awakened mind, thereby clarifying all thoughts and awakening from the agitation of consciousness.
And in the *Samādhi* section: "By means of the pure awakened mind, one realizes that both the nature of the mind and the faculties and their objects are all produced through illusion."
In the *Samādhi-sūtra*, it says: "By means of the pure awakened mind, one does not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness;
one clearly knows that both body and mind are hindrances, and that the luminosity of non-cognition does not depend on any such obstructions.

One should understand that "stillness" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), "illusion" is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and "the luminosity of non-cognition" is the truth of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-satya*). Furthermore, it is said that no object of contemplation is established.

How could the objective realm be attained? How can one claim that because the scriptural text is concise, it is therefore a partial teaching? Master Mi (Mingzhao) once stated in his *Chan-yuan ch'üan* (Verification of the Source of Chan):

"The teachings of Nanyue and Tiantai, which instruct one to rely on the three truths to cultivate the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, are perfect in their doctrinal meaning, yet they ultimately result in a gradual process.
Only the supreme vehicle Chan transmitted by Bodhidharma—also called the Tathāgata Chan—is sudden."
"To share the same Buddha-body while being fundamentally distinct from all other gates"—alas, these words seem to suppress our Patriarch. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies these three;
in that scripture, each of these three has many names and meanings. Speaking according to their primary significance:

*śamatha* is named "concentration" (*samādhi*), *vipaśyanā* is named "wisdom" (*prajñā*), and *ubhayasama* is named "equanimity. What is now called "stopping and contemplation" (*zhiguan*) is simply another name for concentration and wisdom.

By abandoning both extremes through the union of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: 1. **Stopping by Realizing the Essence** (*tattva-śamatha*): Because one knows that things are a false manifestation produced by the provisional conjunction of causes and conditions, their nature is empty;

thus it is called "realizing the essence. When one raises the condition of deluded thought and attains emptiness, that very emptiness is the true reality; therefore, it is called "stopping by realizing the essence. 2.

**Stopping by Following Conditions through Skillful Means** (*upāya-anu-pratyaya-śamatha*): Because one knows that emptiness is not [mere] emptiness, it is called "skillful means. Through discernment, one follows along with conditions.

Because it is like medicine for a disease, it is said that "following conditions" and "settling the mind" are termed *śamatha* (calm abiding) because they accord with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the cessation that stills the conceptualization of the two extremes:

knowing that the conventional is not the conventional, the extreme of the conventional is quiescent; and likewise, not apprehending the non-conventional, the extreme of emptiness is quiescent—therefore, it is called the cessation that stills the two extremes.
This is explained in detail in the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Although these two names differ, they refer to the same [practice], namely, *vipaśyanā* (insight).

*Pāyubhiḥ* and *samādhi*. Regarding the statement that "their essence is also the same," this means that the second [stage] takes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its object, while the third takes the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) as its object.
However, one should know that in the lower *dhyāna*, there is a fusion with the third;

both the simultaneous negation (*dvaya-niṣedha*) and the simultaneous illumination (*dvaya-avabhāsa*) constitute the essence and function of the Middle Way, wherein essence and function mutually manifest one another.

There is no distinction made as to why the second [type of cessation] is not mentioned, for it is easily understood. How could the Great Samādhi (*mahāsamādhi*) be anything other than the three types of cessation?

This is a rhetorical question intended to clarify that this samādhi must necessarily possess the three cessations. Why? Because "samādhi" is itself "cessation," and cessation must rely upon the Truths (*satya*).
If the Truths were not threefold, the encompassing of all phenomena would not be universal. Thus, the title of the sutra says it "is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices. This is excellent.

It is here that [the distinction] lies. Regarding the differentiation between what is primary and what is subordinate, the *Zhiguan* states: "Various sūtras, in accordance with conditions, single out one dharma to demonstrate the starting point of their meaning.
For example, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* singles out the aspect of stillness (*śamatha*) while encompassing all dharmas;

the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* single out the aspect of insight (*vipaśyanā*) while encompassing all dharmas; and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* mentions the three dharmas by the name 'Secret Treasury' (*guhyakośa*). Thus, Tiantai...
Although the referent is indeed the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, its name and meaning cannot differ eternally from the present one.
Regarding the "profound correspondence with the holy words," the Master Zhiyi stated that when he was expounding on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he had not yet heard this scripture. He once remarked:

"The names of these three types of *śamatha* have not been seen in the sūtras or śāstras; they are established according to their meaning in relation to the three types of *vipaśyanā*. If one can seek out the names within the sūtras, then [the correspondence is established]."

This perfectly accords with that meaning. Now, observing the evidence of sincerity, the exposition of the Wise One and the request of Ānanda are as if two halves of a tally fitting together in secret.
Question: Since the names such as *śamatha* and so forth differ from those such as "stopping that accords with reality" (*t'i chen chih*) and so forth, how can they be said to fit together in secret?
Answer: In the past, Master Dao’an’s threefold classification and the threefold classification of Bandhuprabha (Prokṣapāla) also differed in their terminology, yet [the former] preceded [the latter].

Master De praised it, saying: "The wondrous principle is subtly pervasive, and the wise mind is loftily in accord; how could the title 'Pervading the Heavens' (Miyen) be anything other than true? Viewed from this perspective, the three stages of cessation are in profound harmony with the [text];

why then should one find fault with it? Regarding the general and specific requests: the general request aims to correctly open up understanding, while the specific request aims to correctly clarify practice.
Furthermore, the general request is intended for those of the three faculties, while the specific request is intended for those of middling and inferior faculties. Moreover, it is general...
Regarding these eighteen *dhātus*, they are distinguished individually according to each sense organ and object, and also collectively across the ten directions;
since this has already been established from the perspective of this world-system, there is no need for further elaboration here.

Second, as for the phrase "at that time" (*tasmin samaye*), the great assembly’s desire to hear the sutra and those from the ten directions: previously, only the assembly of those who heard it together was listed.
In this context, because the śrāvakas are now being distinguished [from others], it says "the great arhats of the ten directions. As for the question:

"Since the pratyekabuddhas were already described previously as 'immeasurable,' why are they listed again? The answer is: since it says "at that time there were also," this phrase should be read as heading the following section.
Thus, those previously assembled had already heard the introductory discourse of the sutra, whereas those who have now arrived are only now hearing it.
The formal exposition.
Third, the Buddha’s discourse below is divided into three parts: first, opening up the *Lengyan* to explain the awakened mind; second, revealing the *Lengyan* methods of practice;
and third, indicating the stages and positions of the *Lengyan*. That all these sections take *Lengyan* as their title is because [the author] did not forget its origin.
The fundamental structure is as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as categorized by Zhàngān, where all five sections are titled with "Nirvāṇa. Now, I shall follow that precedent.

Second, the section "Furthermore, below" refutes the notion of non-conjunction, which has two parts: first, a general application of the rules for both the specific and the universal as before; second, the specific [refutation] starting from "If these two were not... [and so forth].

The refutation further consists of two parts: first, the difficulty in clarifying the conditions for conjunction. The *Sūtra* asks: "How does one clearly distinguish between the principle of conjunction and the principle of non-conjunction?

Section Two: Ānanda’s Inquiry at the Lower Assembly; Refuting the Aggregates and Entrances to Clarify the Emptiness of Dharmas. This section is divided into two parts: first, refuting the four dharmas; second, refuting the seven elements.
The first part is further divided into two: first, showing the true nature of phenomena. The Sūtra says: "Regarding the various marks of illusion and transformation, the *Jñāna-śāstra* states:

'For example, like illusory elephants, horses, and various other objects, although one knows they have no reality, they can still be seen and heard. [Commentary on the Sūtra passage] Section on the Land (Kṣetra).
That which does not reach [another] perishes in a single *kṣaṇa*, arising and ceasing without before or after; because it does not reach another, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"I teach the meaning of *kṣaṇa* as the non-arising of all dharmas; that what arises at the very first moment is simultaneously subject to cessation—this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant.

Second, regarding the fact that the Two Vehicles do not fail to destroy phenomena: the Two Vehicles of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) schools practice the analytical and essential [methods of deconstruction].

The contemplation [of emptiness] also refutes the notion of the five aggregates as substantial dharmas; since the meaning for small *bodhisattvas* is the same as that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is not explained separately.

As for the statement that "the *bodhisattva* is not without a self," this refers to the attachment to a self held by those outside the [Buddhist] fold; because their ignorance is not yet exhausted, they still possess the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
This is as the *Bodhisattva Kāśyapa* said in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Prior to this day, we were all called those with false views."

▲ While it may be reasonable to distribute [the categories] in this manner, the ancient masters collectively state that the former "slightly breaks" attachment to persons (*pudgala-grāha*) while the latter "greatly breaks" attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

This is because it is said that the two vehicles have not yet attained the *nirvāṇa* of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), whereas Bodhisattvas have already attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) within the realm.

The same principle applies to attachment to phenomena; that is, the delusions of the upper realms and external objects cannot be considered the same as the delusions of thought (*kleśa*) of the two vehicles.
This is a categorization. ▲ Regarding the threefold distinctions based on the dull faculties (*mūḍhendriya*) and individual inclinations (*pranidhāna*), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"Aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are [defined as] collections, birth-gates, and lineages; because there are three types of dullness, faculties, and inclinations, the aggregates, bases, and elements are taught.
Now, regarding the three types of dullness: first, for those who are dull regarding the mind, the five aggregates are taught; this opens the mind into four [aggregates] and combines form into one.
For those of dull faculties who regard form as primary, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are taught;

therein, form is expanded into ten and a half bases—namely, the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and a portion of the mental object-base (*dharmāyatana*)—while mind is condensed into one and a half bases—namely, the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and a portion of the mental object-base.

For those of dull faculties who regard both mind and form as primary, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are taught; therein, mind is further expanded into seven and a half elements—namely, the six consciousnesses and the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

It is said that the faculties (*indriya*), the objects of cognition (*viṣaya*), and a portion of the dharmas are all delusions of the ignorant. Regarding the "three faculties," they refer to superior, middling, and inferior;
regarding the "three joys," they refer to concise, middling, and extensive—these are respectively assigned to the three categories.

As for the statement that "the fruit consists of the three bodies while the causal principle contains them," this means that the cause—the mind of sentient beings—is endowed with the three Buddha-natures, which thus contain and encompass the three bodies. Regarding the phrase "without the marks of the two extremes," it refers to the Perfect [Teaching].
The Master takes the three pairs—coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death—as the characteristics of the two extremes.

Following this, from "Ānanda, secondly," he relies on the True to refute the false, which constitutes four sections: first, refuting the five aggregates; second, refuting the six sense bases; third, refuting the twelve bases;

and fourth, refuting the eighteen elements. The first of these [the five aggregates] is further divided into two parts: first, a general restatement; second, from "Ānanda" onwards, a specific refutation.

Furthermore, there are five [sections]: from the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The first [section] has two parts: first, revealing delusion through a metaphor; second, using that metaphor to break through attachments.
The first part has two sub-sections: first, the metaphor. In the Sutra, it says "staring until fatigue arises. The *Pīcāng* states: "Staring means looking straight ahead.
Regarding "seeing illusory forms such as floating hairs or a second moon," Changshui says: "One may see things such as circles of hair or a double moon. [End of] Note.
The manifestation of the forms of the nine realms is explained here provisionally from the perspective of delusion;

it is not that the causes and fruits of the Buddha-realm lack the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), but because one realizes that form is but mind, it is not mentioned. II. The Dharma of the Aggregate of Form and Below. ▲ The Sūtra is likewise so;

this must be understood by correlating it with the preceding and following textual contexts to reveal its meaning. Since the preceding section has already used the metaphor of "wild flowers" to represent [deluded perceptions],...
In the subsequent passage concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it says: "These various delusive flowers do not come from space," and so forth;

this precisely serves as a metaphor for how the aggregate of form does not arise from causes and conditions. Since the text of the analogy is already detailed, the phenomenon being illustrated is explained very briefly, its phrasing being skillfully placed in between.
The latter four aggregates may be understood by analogy with this. △ Second, from "Ānanda" onwards...

This is an analogy for breaking through attachments, which is further divided into two parts: first, breaking [the notion of] other-nature by means of the phrase "not coming from emptiness," and breaking self-nature by means of the phrase "not emerging from itself.

Speaking in terms of dharmas, one should distinguish between self and other based on the mind and its objects. Generally, the remaining four aggregates (*skandhas*) all possess both the meanings of self and other;

it is because these are included within the four natures that they are treated briefly here while being refuted. Only within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is there a departure from self.

Question: Since other interpretations seem to refute the nature of causelessness (*ahetutva*), and since the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* refutes the two attachments to person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*), why is it necessary to refute the four modes of being (*catur-koṭi*)?

Furthermore, among these four modes, why is there a greater emphasis on refuting the "self" (*svataḥ*) and "other" (*parataḥ*) modes? Answer: Jingxi says: "The four modes of being are the root of all views;

'self' and 'other' are, in turn, the roots of the 'joint' (*ubhayataḥ*) and 'causeless' (*ahetutaḥ*) modes. This is why it is so. Thus, for the sake of those to be converted, the Venerable Nāgārjuna..."

The faculties of people in these later times have become increasingly dull; thus, [Nāgārjuna] extensively composed the *Mādhyamaka-śāstra* as a method of contemplation, taking the investigation of the fourfold nature (*catuskoṭi*) as its fundamental principle.

This is precisely in accord with the present sutra and serves as the final model for future generations. May those who expound this sutra not neglect its detailed textual elaborations. Thus, regarding Ānanda:
first, the preceding meaning was specifically designated, and then he was summoned and refuted. The remainder should all be understood by following this pattern. [The character] "yì" (翳).
The *Guangya* states that [the character] means "to obstruct" (*zhàng*) and "to suddenly" (*yǎn*). △ Second, from "Therefore" (*shìgù*) onwards is the conclusion.

Thus, one knows that although the intent of this conclusion is to exclude what is not [the truth], it does not directly manifest the meaning established previously. △ Second, from "Ānanda" onwards, [the text discusses] the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The section headings are the same as before. Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, "For example, there is a person whose hands and feet are relaxed," the *Sung-shu* (Commentary) states:
"This uses a near matter to illustrate a remote principle; it is both a dharma and a metaphor. The character "譬" (*pi*) already contains a partial metaphor. Now I say:

if this were so, would it be only the preceding [passage on] the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) that uses the term "for example"? The subsequent passages concerning the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and others all likewise state "for example. Thus, they are all metaphors.
One may say that by using the near to illustrate the distant, one should know that although this passage speaks in terms of concrete phenomena (*vastu*), its underlying intent lies in analogy.

As for the section beginning with "up to the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), although the word "analogy" (*dṛṣṭānta*) appears, it actually refutes [the self] by means of the characteristics of phenomena themselves.

Regarding the phrase "suddenly as if forgetting birth," there is an error where some have written "forgetting delusion" (*wang sheng*) instead of "forgetting birth. *Zhengzhen* says: "Forgetting birth" is synonymous with "forgetting form"; it means—

When the hundred members of the body are in harmony, one does not associate with sensations such as suffering, pleasure, sorrow, or joy; dwelling in tranquil stillness, it is as if there were no physical form or life.
Yet, in the letter Li Ling sent to Su Wu, he says: "Whenever a thought arises, I suddenly forget my very life. The commentary to the *Wenxuan* states:
"Suddenly one is unaware that life has a state of being born. The present translator has indeed employed this expression, making only a slight modification.
Yet, it is "as-it-is" (*tathatā*). Regarding the anecdote that "when talking of pickled plums, water flows from the mouth," the *Shishuo xinyu* states:
When Emperor Wu of Wei lost his way while on campaign, the entire army was parched with thirst. The Emperor ordered his men to say, "Ahead there is a large plum tree with many fruits;

they are sweet and sour and can quench thirst. Upon hearing this, the soldiers' mouths all began to water. Note: If the two characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) were distinct, both would have to manifest simultaneously.
Changshui says: "It is like a tree producing fruit; the fruit is not the tree, yet both are present now. This is not yet the case.
▲ If the sutra were to separate from emptiness, this would be like being without a cause. ▲ "Using it to send to another country" means to provide offerings.
Holding an empty vessel is like using a container filled with food to go and offer it to another country. ▲ The commentary states: "The consciousness that sustains the body through karma."

Changshui says that when the moment of death arrives, the sense faculties become obstructed, as if the two apertures were blocked. Are these two explanations correct?
