Third Fascicle, Part Two: Refuting the Six Entrances (Ṣaḍāyatana). Section One: General Summary. Now, regarding the "six entrances" (ṣaḍāyatana), there are generally two meanings:

first, that the faculties and their objects mutually enter into one another; second, that both the faculties and the objects are what consciousness enters into. For this reason, various sūtras refer to them as the "ten [entrances]."
The second is the *āyatana* (entrances). Now, this sutra designates only the six sense organs (*indriya*) as the six entrances;

this is because the organs possess a superior significance, being capable of directly generating consciousness, and because the organs can receive objects and draw forth the external sensory fields (*viṣaya*). Therefore, they alone are specifically called "entrances. As the text below states:

"The six [organs] act as intermediaries for thieves, robbing one of the family's treasures. And the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "The village of the six entrances is where the bandits of the fetters dwell. All of these refer to this.
This is the meaning. △ Second, the specific refutation by Ānanda and others is divided into six parts: from the first eye-āyatana up to the sixth mind-āyatana. First, there are two further sections:
(1) pointing to a phenomenon and using it as a metaphor for delusion. ▲ Note:

Regarding the statement that the preceding text’s metaphorical sense-forgans (*indriya*) are taken here as the phenomena being illustrated—Question: If this is so, what serves as the metaphor in this context? Answer: It is the same.
The "dazed eyes giving rise to the appearance of fatigue" (*bodhi-staimitya-kleśa-lakṣaṇa*) is the analogy; however, this analogy is expressed in terms of the phenomena it illustrates.

"Bodhi" is awakening; from awakening, delusion arises, just as dazed eyes give rise to fatigue. The meaning of the Sūtra is that the eye and the fatigue mentioned within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are likewise the appearance of fatigue arising from the dazing of awakened clarity.
The appearance of fatigue is like a flower in the sky (*gaganapuşpa*). One should know that the preceding...

The metaphor of "empty flowers" (*śūnya-puṣpa*) pervading the nine realms refers to the forms perceived by the five sense organs; here, the "empty flowers" specifically represent the characteristics of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) within the nine realms.
The former is broad while the latter is narrow, and they must not be conflated. The examples of "plugging the ears to hear sounds" and so forth are likewise like this;
for instance, the "fatigued eyes" are all easily understood as delusive phenomena. Regarding Master Yuan’s interpretation, its meaning... [is as follows].
Otherwise, one would be using that which is to be illustrated as the illustration itself. △ Second, refuting attachment based on the following [text] regarding delusion has two parts:
first, showing the nature of delusion. ▲ In the sūtra, "two kinds of delusive objects" refers back to the fatigued eyes;

this is cited according to the condition of light to demonstrate their delusive characteristics. Light must exist in contrast to darkness; they are established through mutual dependence. Thus, this seeing does not exist apart from its objects.
In terms of their true nature (*dharmatā*), all sense-bases (*āyatana*) such as the eye are equally false; the same principle applies to the ear and the other bases.
When the lecturer reaches the following section, he must clarify this meaning. II. Refuting Attachment to Sentiment (from "In this way" onwards) has two parts:
A. Refutation. ▲ Scripture: "It does not emerge from the faculties to realize the Truth. Question: Here, the primary refutation concerns the faculties (*indriya*); why then do you now say "no"?

If it were the case that [consciousness] arises from the sense organs (*indriya*), how would this differ from the refutation of consciousness? Answer: When we speak here of "the organs," we are merely referring to their own essential nature (*svabhāva*).
To say that all phenomena do not arise from themselves is precisely this meaning. [Objection: This is not so.

Above, you spoke of the "nature of seeing" (*darśana-svabhāva*), and below, you spoke of the "nature of hearing" (*śravaṇa-svabhāva*), even extending to the "nature of cognition" (*vijñapti-svabhāva*) regarding the mind-base (*manāyatana*). This "nature" (*svabhāva*) is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*). If...
If it were not consciousness (*vijñāna*), how could there be the sense of seeing or hearing when the various faculties have not yet produced consciousness?

You should know that those who refute the faculties by inferring [the existence of] consciousness do so because the arising and ceasing of the six present faculties are difficult to perceive; thus, they infer from the various consciousnesses and thereby refute them.
Since each consciousness does not arise independently, how can it be established? It is, for example, like the roots of grass and trees which are able to produce branches.

The leaves are merely named "roots," and when the branches and leaves die, one knows the roots have already withered; by this analogy, the general intent of contemplating phenomena (*dharma*) can be seen. Question:
If that is so, it would suffice in meaning to refute only the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); why is it necessary to refute all six bases (*āyatana*) and twelve bases as well? Answer:

This is because the various real entities (*bhāva*) as they are conceptually constructed differ; thus, three categories are established. However, when it comes to the actual investigation and refutation, [the same logic applies].
It must be explained by combining these three points. Regarding the statement that "it is distinct when viewed from the perspective of itself," Changshui says:
"It may also be because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is viewed in relation to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Thus it is called 'root-born,' further increasing the flavor of others.
"Does not arise from emptiness" refers to realizing the Truth; this phrase refutes arising without a cause (*ahetuka*). "Did not emerge from the sense-faculties" refutes arising from self (*svataḥ*).

If "arising" does not come from light or darkness to destroy other-arising, then three propositions are established. If one were to combine self-arising and other-arising to form a "common nature," that would be the meaning of the fourth proposition.
Question: In the previous discussion of the five aggregates, you recorded emptiness as "other-arising. Now, in realizing the truth, why do you treat emptiness as being without cause? Answer:
Generally, the meaning of the four natures is distinguished according to the specific textual context; it cannot be restricted to a single fixed definition.
In the preceding passage, because it was established that there is no separate "other-nature" (parabhāva) external to emptiness, emptiness could be taken as the "other.
Since empty space is also an object perceived by the eye-faculty, the present text’s mention of light and darkness allows for the possibility of "arising from another";
thus, taking emptiness as the causeless "other" is highly convenient in meaning. △ Second, "Therefore... concludes [the section]. △ Second, "Ānanda... begins the section on the ear-faculty.
The analysis of the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) up to this point is the same as before. ▲ Note: Regarding the phrase "not taking the meaning of comparison":

although the two characters *pì* (comparison) and *yù* (metaphor) may be divided for the time being—as in the *Fahua shu*, where "comparison" (*bǐkàng*) is taken as *pì* and "instruction" (*xiǎoxùn*) is taken as *yù*—if one speaks generally, as in the *Shōmon-ron* (Śrāvaka-bhūmi), "comparison" (*pì*) is itself the "metaphor" (*yù*). Following this general sense here, the term "comparison" (*bǐkàng*) is not adopted.
▲ Those who went there traveled from Xingfu to Changshui.

▲ This refers to the previous discussion regarding the "carrying down of Li" (the *Xielǐ* commentary), which states that the current scripture’s explanation of Huajing and Mingwen as manifestations of the permanence of nature is based on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) found in the subsequent passage: "Sound has its own arising and ceasing within hearing;
it is not that your hearing-nature is existent or non-existent. ▲ The scripture is urgent and restrictive.

Its nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) is like a contraction. Regarding "penetration and obstruction" (*saṃvṛta-vivṛta*) and "emptiness and solidity" (*śūnya-sāra*): penetration and obstruction refer to the objects (*viṣaya*), while emptiness and solidity refer to the faculties (*indriya*).

When the faculty is empty, the object penetrates; when the faculty is solid, the object is obstructed. Regarding the two objects of "separation and union" and "opposition and compliance": when the body and its environment meet, there is opposition and compliance.

Compliance refers to the smooth and supple (*ślakṣṇa-mṛdu*), while opposition refers to the coarse and rough (*karkaśa-kaṭhina*). Because it does not meet with the environment, it is called [the faculty].

"To be separated from the two objects" means to be separated from both union and disjunction. Since the Sūtra does not arise through union or disjunction, this refutes co-arising (*sahotpāda*), because "separation" also implies an object.
Because there is neither contrariety nor conformity, it refutes arising from another (*parabhava*). Because it does not emerge from the sense faculties, it refutes arising from self (*svabhava*).

Furthermore, because it does not arise from emptiness, it is not causeless (*ahetuka*). [Note: Regarding the "five fallen-away sensory objects," the *Abhidharma* calls them "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*). It is also...

Regarding "invisible and non-obstructive form" (*anidarśana-apratigha-rūpa*), the *Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas* (*Bai fa shu*) states that the five sense organs, such as the eye, only take present objects as their conditions.

It says: "The first five evolving consciousnesses take the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as their objects; because these are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they take the real and not the provisional.

'Real' refers to blue and so forth; 'provisional' refers to length and so forth. Regarding "flowing into a place beyond the reach of the five sense organs," Zizhong says: "The eyes and ears [take...]"
External sensory objects flow momentarily into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*); entering from the outside into the inside is called "gushing flow.

The first part is further divided into two: first, citing phenomena to examine their nature. The Sūtra says: "The nature of space is formless; it is manifested through form. The *Yuan* commentary states: "Both space and form are provisional;
they exist in mutual dependence, and their substance is not separate from form. Therefore, the Hīnayāna takes light and darkness as its substance. The Mahāyāna [takes it otherwise].

The essence [of space] consists of the color of "one-void" (ekavarṇa) and the color of extreme remoteness (prāntakoṭika). (Seeing the void above is called the color of "manifested space" [varṇākāśa]; seeing the void below is called the color of "remoteness" [koṭyākāśa]). Guishan said:
"Ordinary people falsely cling to the notion that space is form (*rūpa*), and so forth; this is refuted in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter on Kāśyapa.

Alternatively, some cite the Dharma-characteristics school (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to claim that space is entirely form; this completely背离 (contradicts) the fundamental tenet of the sūtra. Now, I shall rescue this from Zizhong regarding the 'space' of this sūtra."
First establishing [the position] and subsequently refuting it, the same applies to *nirvāṇa* and space. How is this clarified?

In that sutra, the Buddha says, "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space"—this is the establishment [of the position]. Kāśyapa then contrasts space with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), asserting that space is an existent;
therefore, the Buddha uses ten successive arguments to refute his error, fearing that [Kāśyapa’s view] might lead to misunderstanding.
Sentient beings identify the nature of the metaphor (the object illustrated) as being identical to the emptiness that serves as the illustration; this is precisely what is being refuted.
When it is now said that the nature of emptiness is formless, this merely means that it lacks the forms of the environment and its inhabitants (the supported and the support).

Nevertheless, because the characteristics of the great expanse of emptiness are manifested through the colors of the environment and its inhabitants, it is said that "emptiness is manifested by means of form. This, then, correctly takes the emptiness of *nirvāṇa* as the illustration, and is not [the emptiness of mere non-existence].
Because it is formless, the subsequent passage states that "digging a well and finding empty space" refers to the category of *pratyag-rūpa* (distant or pervasive form).

Furthermore, the preceding text says, "Even though empty space has names and appearances," and the following text says, "seeing and awareness are as insentient as empty space. Thus, how could this "insentient emptiness" (*pṛthivī-ākāśa*) be without form?
One should understand that when this sutra speaks of emptiness as being "great," it does so to clarify that empty space exists due to deluded ignorance.
The world is established based on space; furthermore, it is said that when one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, this space of the ten directions is entirely dissolved.

For this reason, the element of space must be explained immediately after the four great elements, as it is established here first. It is only when we proceed to the later text and analyze it through the threefold negation that it constitutes a refutation.
Guishan used the principle of refutation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to explain this initial establishment of the principle, yet he still criticized [the interpretation of] Yuan.
It is an error for the Master to claim that the entire purport of the Sūtras is [contradicted] here. Regarding the commentary on the four castes beginning with Kṣatriya:

it relies entirely upon the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) for its explanation. Guxiang says: "Kṣatriya is translated here as 'Lord of the Fields' (*tiānzhǔ*), which corresponds to the emperors and kings of this land.

"Successive generations" (*yìshì*) means, as the saying goes, "successing the lineage. "Benevolence and forbearance" (*rénshù*): to measure things with one's own mind is called "forbearance" (*shù*). As for "conduct" (*cāo*), it refers to...
Conduct. ▲ A merchant is one who travels while selling; a peddler is one who sits and sells. ▲ "Trade" (*mào*) refers to extensive exchange.

▲ "Migration" (*qiān*) means shifting and changing; it involves buying where there is abundance and selling where there is scarcity, seeking profit from both far and near, pursuing gain wherever it may be found without discrimination.
▲ "Market stall" (*sì*) means displaying goods for sale. "Fields" (*chóu*) refers to the ridges and furrows of the land. ▲ Regarding those superior at farming, "planting" (*zhǒng*) is said to be...
Reaping the harvest is called *saka*. Regarding the divergence of the clear and turbid streams: the Kṣatriyas, who practice pure conduct, are of noble lineage, like a clear stream;
the Vaiśyas and Śūdras are of lowly lineage, like a turbid stream. Regarding the non-communication of marriages: the noble and the lowly each marry within their own respective classes.
Regarding the different paths for flying and hiding: according to the regulations of the Western Land (India), those of noble and lowly lineage each follow their own way when they travel.
When traveling on the road, they stay in different places. △ Second, from "Ānanda" downward, the refutation of attachments according to their inclinations.

▲ In the sutra, from "If it arises from the earth" downward, the refutation has two meanings: first, the refutation based on the difference between space and earth; second, from "If there is no entering or exiting" downward, the refutation based on the identity between space and earth.
△ Second, from "If this" downward, revealing the reality, which again has two parts: first, showing the true nature; second, censuring the heterodox.
The first explanation further has three parts. First, a category that pervades all the "Greats" (mahā). [Note: The phrase "Or perhaps" below refers to Changshui. He says:

"Now, what is called 'Great' has the meaning of being eternal and pervasive. Being eternal, it is without arising, ceasing, or movement; being pervasive, it exists in all times and places... even to the point of saying:
because it is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, it is named 'Great'. Second, from "Ānanda" onwards, there is the reprimand for delusion.
Mind. △ Third, from "You [should know] entirely" onwards, the true nature is correctly demonstrated. ▲ In the Sūtra, "The nature of awakening is true emptiness;

the nature of emptiness is true awakening," the former phrase is the absolute within the conventional, and the latter phrase is the conventional within the absolute. △ Second, from "The world" onwards, false doctrines are refuted.

From "Ānanda, the great element of the sense-faculties" down to "the great element of consciousness," the structural divisions are as previously described. ▲ Commentary: "Awakening to touch and awakening to cognition."

The claim that "all belong to the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*)"—meaning that when the body-faculty perceives touch and gives rise to discrimination, it then belongs to the mind-faculty—is likely incorrect.
Therefore, I privately maintain that the sutra can be interpreted differently to establish what exists and preclude what does not exist. The *Jingchao* states:

"The first phrase refers to form (*rūpa*), and the second phrase refers to space (*ākāśa*). To further distinguish these two within the preceding object-field clarifies the distinction between light-and-dark as form and space."

This means: "Consciousness is active and seeing is still; they are neither blended nor conjoined. This refers to their lack of blending and conjunction based on the mutual opposition between the activity of the sense-faculties and consciousness and the stillness of seeing.

If one considers this in relation to external objects, it likewise refutes the theory of self-arising. As stated in the section on the element of wind: "Wind and space are separated by their natures; they are neither blended nor conjoined.
Since this is discussed in contrast to objects, it still refutes the theory of other-arising. As for the section on the element of fire: [it says...]
The sun and its reflection are far apart; they neither harmonize nor unite. This is precisely the mutual observation of self and other, which serves to destroy the nature of harmony.
This is explained according to the specific meaning [of the context], and thus it is not a single approach.
Second, from "At that time" onwards, there are two parts: first, the narrator’s account of the events; second, Ānanda’s recitation of verses.

The first section further consists of two parts, the first of which describes the realization of the mind. Regarding the commentary stating that "the ten directions" (*daśadig*) refers to the "ten realms" (*daśadhātu*):

the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one shines universally throughout the ten directions. Because sin and merit reside within sentient beings, the Master Zhiyi explained "directions" (*dig*) as referring to the "realms" (*dhātu*) of sentient beings.
Here, however, it is said that "the mind pervades the ten directions," using "directions" in the sense of spatial location; this will be addressed later in the section on "all things."

The "world" and so forth refer to the self-inclusion of sentient beings; how much more so for those who are deluded and confused! There is an emptiness upon which [the world] relies, and within this emptiness, realms are established, forming a distinct sequence.

Let the student examine this carefully. II. From "Paying Homage to the Buddha" downward, the section describes the characteristics of reverence. II. The section on Ānanda’s recitation of verses is divided into four parts.
First, praising the virtues and describing the benefits. Regarding the two lines that praise the virtues: first, he praises the Teacher who is able to preach; second, he praises what is preached.
The Practice of the Dharma. ▲ Note: This is one of the Ten Epithets of the Venerable One, according to the *Śāstra*.
If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Ratnavali*, the ten epithets range from "Tathāgata" to "Buddha. Possessing these ten titles, he is named the Honored One of the World;

this is because "Unsurpassed Being" (*Anuttara-puruṣa*) and "Charioteer of Men" (*Puruṣa-damya-sārathi*) are treated as two separate titles. Guishan states that these are the three virtues praised [in him].

This fruit realized by the Buddha was attained through the cultivation of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) within the causal stage, whereby the essence of the mind became still and luminous;

therefore, Ānanda’s previous request for the "wonderful *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi" was essentially a request for the causes of the Tathāgata’s own practice, which he now wishes to rely upon for his own cultivation and study. Having already received this instruction, [he continues:]

Because one awakens to the eternal mind, one returns to praising the Buddha by means of the fruits of the three virtues (triguṇa) achieved through the causes of the three contemplations (trivipaśyanā).
The meaning of this sequential interlocking is as follows. Question: Since the "principle" (li) is that which is realized through profound stillness, how can it be called *Lengyan*?
Answer: It is analogous to saying that both wisdom (*jñāna*) and the object of that wisdom (*jñeyaviṣaya*) are both termed *prajñā*.

What prevents us from saying that both "samādhi" (concentration) and the "site of samādhi" are both called *Lengyan*? Furthermore, as in the section on *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only), the Master Yuan has fully cited the Three Teachings—the *Āgama* (Zang), *Vaipulya* (Tong), and *Pratyekabuddha* (Bie)—to conduct this comparative analysis.
The previous citation from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* refers to the *Āgama* Teaching;

next, he cites the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to clarify that the seventh stage is equal to the Arhat, while the eighth stage sustains residual habits (*vāsanā*) to moisten rebirth for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

Thereafter, attaining Buddhahood constitutes the *tongjiao* (Common Teaching). Later, the *Weishi* (Consciousness-Only) doctrine is cited to clarify the meaning of the *biejiao* (Distinct Teaching); the intermediate stages are here omitted.
Regarding the "partial realization of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind," Master Yuan’s commentary states:

"Based on this state, it should correspond to what is realized by those who have ascended to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) in the *biejiao*, or by those at the initial dwelling in the *yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching). Furthermore, the subsequent interpretation is certainly not the intent of the Sutra; it cites the *Huayan*...
Regarding the strict classification of these matters as being dissimilar, one must rely on the verse which states, "not passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*," etc.

Question: Can this principle be applied to the initial stage of a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*)? Answer: There is no impediment to explaining it in such a way. As the preceding text states:

"If one can transform objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata. Guishan also distinguished this by means of the six stages of realization (*liu ji*). Since what is described in the present text pertains to the era of the Buddha, [it is appropriate].
The assembly present at that time must be interpreted as having attained partial realization of the *dharmakāya*. Regarding the passage "Although Ānanda was among the assembly," etc.:
even if he had not yet attained true realization, he should have been one who had attained a semblance of it; why then was he ensnared by Māra at the time of *nirvāṇa*?
In the thirty-sixth fascicle of that sutra, the Buddha asks Cunda: "Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now? Cunda replied: "He is..."
Outside the Śāla grove, Ānanda was harassed by sixty-four trillion māras.
All these hosts of māras transformed themselves into the likeness of the Tathāgata, preaching various dharmas and even manifesting supernatural powers and transformations.
Having seen this, Ānanda thought to himself: "I have never before seen such a divine transformation; whose work is this?"
Was it not the World-Honored One Śākyamuni who acted? Yet, whenever he wished to rise or speak, his will was never fulfilled.

At that time, Mañjuśrī received a dhāraṇī from the Buddha and went to Ānanda; having recited the mantra, the Māra kings and their retinues gave rise to the bodhicitta, abandoned their demonic activities, and immediately released Ānanda to come before the Buddha.
[The character *jiǔ* (罥) is pronounced *gǔ* with the *fǎ* (法) tone; it means "to bind" or "to capture."]

△ Second, “I vow now” and below is the section on making vows to repay kindness. Changshui says: “Because one expects to attain the realization of the fruit within this very body, it is said ‘I vow now.
I, however, say that ‘now’ is a term referring to oneself; for the supreme fruit of wondrous enlightenment cannot be grasped within this immediate body.

△ Third, “I humbly entreat” and below is the section on requesting testimony and seeking empowerment, which is further divided into two parts. First, requesting testimony regarding the transformation of others. ▲

The commentary on the aspiration to take up earth states: "As in the case of Śākyamuni’s 'Valley Resonance,' according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Ānanda was given the prediction that he would become a Buddha in the future named Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña-rāja. Since that has already been explained, it is not mentioned here.
However, what is clarified therein concerns a pure land; therefore, it says, 'His buddha-field is pure and is named Constantly Erected Victorious Banner. Now...

Why is it that one vows to take up a defiled land? Now, when the eternal mind is realized, even empty space perishes; since there is only the single, fundamental, wondrous purity, who can discuss "pure" and "defiled"?
It is only in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings that distinctions arise. When the ultimate goal is discussed, the Way of every Buddha is equal.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states: "One should know that Śākyamuni Buddha further possesses a pure land."
In the land of Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha likewise possesses an unadorned and impure land, just as Śākyamuni Buddha’s land does;
since both Amitābha and Śākyamuni each have both pure and impure lands, why must Ānanda harbor doubts regarding these two different accounts in the sūtras concerning the taking of soil?
Furthermore, this passage states that he first entered the impure land and subsequently took soil from the pure land; thus, the meaning is all the more consistent.
Know that returning to observe the world is like an event within a dream; who can distinguish between the purity and defilement, or the superiority and inferiority, of the lands seen in a dream?
It is hoped that future generations will attempt to contemplate this principle. II. Seeking the empowerment for one’s own practice from the Great Hero (the Buddha).

The Fourth Fascicle begins, Part Two:
The Section on Revealing the Non-Empty Tathāgatagarbha by Resolving the Two Doubts regarding Nature and Characteristics with Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, consisting of three parts:

First, the Narrator describes the ritual setting; Second, from "Great Power" onwards, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra sets forth his intention, which is divided into four sections: First, praising the person and the Dharma; Second, from "World-Honored One" onwards... [text continues].

The description of self and others has two parts; the first describes the self. Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "Among those who preach the Dharma, I am the foremost," this is said from the perspective of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the note that "the original text does not appear to have seen [this]," this is also spoken from the perspective of the wisdom-eye of the past.

The second part, "The World-Honored One and below," describes others. Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "Those among our assembly who have ascended to the state of outflowlessness," this describes those of the same class.

Among them, many were Dharma-body Mahāsattvas who concealed their original nature and manifested traces to guide those of lesser capacity, such as Pūrṇa, who had already received the prediction of future Buddhahood with the name Dharmaprabhāsa at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Question:

If we discuss them according to their manifested traces, Ānanda was at the stage of the first fruit and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was at the stage of no-more-learning; yet, in the preceding text, it says that Ānanda had already attained awakening—why is this so?

"Does Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and the others still harbor lingering doubts and regrets? Answer: "It is not meant that they were enlightened previously and now have no doubts, nor that they doubt now because they had not been enlightened before.
Rather, these teachings were proclaimed by questioning the Buddha based on the characteristics arising from their state of non-enlightenment.

As for this single period [of teaching], if one observes these two individuals, there is indeed a difference in the degree of their delusion regarding the principle. Why is this? Ānanda, from the beginning, relied upon the dual attachments to persons and dharmas."
The delusion regarding the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is heavy; Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra harbors dual doubts concerning both its nature (*svabhāva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The delusion regarding the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is light. Furthermore, the principle of the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is relatively easy to clarify, whereas the meaning of the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is difficult to comprehend.
For this reason, Ānanda first gave rise to [doubts] at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), while Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra did not.

In the *Xue* (Commentary), it is said that those who attained awakening previously were of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, whereas those who have not yet awakened now are of middling or inferior capacity.

I say this is not so. When the Dharma is preached in various sutras, if it is intended for those of middling or inferior capacity, there must be a sense of circumstantiality and gradual accommodation.
For instance, in the *Lotus Sutra*, through the two cycles of the Parable and the Causes and Conditions, the provisional teachings are opened up and the ultimate reality is revealed; even though...

This is not different from what was taught in the *Dharmapada*; however, while the previous analogies were somewhat indirect, the meaning of the "Non-Empty Treasury" (*Aśūnyagarbha*) discussed in the present sutra is established in conjunction with the two meanings of the "Empty Treasury" (*Śūnyagarbha*).
Thus, the textual intent becomes increasingly profound and is not easily understood.

This is precisely what Ānanda previously meant when he said, "I hope you will further examine and eliminate even the subtlest delusions. If one were to distinguish between those of sharp and dull faculties here, I fear it would be a misrepresentation.

I once deliberated upon this: if one wishes to distinguish three grades of capacity (*indriya*) within this sutra, then from the point before Ānanda’s request for instruction, although [the teaching] generally applies to all three capacities, those who attained awakening were exclusively of the highest capacity. It was only after his request that it subsequently applied to the middle and lower capacities.
Furthermore, within the practice itself there is both the primary and the auxiliary; thus, the primary may be considered the middle, and the auxiliary the lower.
...and so forth. △ Regarding the section "The Three Honored Ones" below, there are two parts concerning the nature and characteristics of doubt.
First, the doubt regarding how the *ālaya-vijñāna* (store-consciousness) gives rise to the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness). ▲ The Sūtra asks: "How does it suddenly arise?

Although the preceding text stated that [the mind] "accords with the minds of sentient beings, responds to the scope of what is known, and manifests according to karma," this was spoken in general and abbreviated terms; furthermore, it had not yet clearly explained the reasons for the arising of all phenomena. Therefore, now...

The extensive discussion of doubts concerns the meaning of the nature of the world (*loka-dhātu*) and so forth. The mountains, rivers, and great earth are the *parinirmita* (the environment or dependent retribution);

all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) are the *sambhoga* (the primary retribution). Since both the environment and the primary retribution possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, it is said that they "successively migrate and flow," and so on.

[Section] Two: Furthermore, below, there is a doubt as to how the nature of the Great [Dharma] can be universally pervasive. In the *Cangjie pian*, the term "陵" (*líng*) is explained as "to extinguish."
"Invading" (*qīn*) is sometimes written as "overpowering" (*líng*); their meanings are identical. △ Fourth, from "I only pray" (*wéiyuàn*) onwards, the request for instruction.

second, from "I shall cause you" (*lìngrǔ*) onwards, the indication of the covering. ▲ In the sutra, from "not yet having attained the two emptinesses" (*èrkōng*) onwards, the question regarding the Buddha’s intention to cause [others to attain it].
Question: For one who has not yet attained emptiness but attains it [now], how does this accord with the meaning of the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*?
Answer: It is as when one speaks of "empty flowers" arising from an eye disease; because there is something seen, one knows that the flowers are fundamentally empty.
To speak of the meaning of "non-emptiness" is likewise intended to manifest emptiness. [Note on the Five Natures: The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "First, the nature of the śrāvaka..."
Second, the *pratyekabuddha* lineage; third, the *tathāgata-yāna* lineage; fourth, the indeterminate lineage; and fifth, the absence of lineage (*agotra*), namely the *icchantika*.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* all explain these five lineages as being largely consistent with the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

Guxiang says: "The five lineages consist of three non-existent and two existent; they take Maitreya as their ancestor and Vasubandhu as their master, and [the present work] analyzes the firewood [of these doctrines]."
Xuanzang has fulfilled the compassionate grace [of his teacher] and established a teaching that serves as a lasting model; he considers this his own supreme proclamation.

Now, according to this sutra, we clearly see that it reveals the provisional nature of those [other teachings]. (From the *Chao*) Question: The *Zuanyao* states that while the *Lotus Sutra* and the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* merely transform the indeterminate nature of the two vehicles, this present sutra transforms both the indeterminate and the determinate natures;
therefore, it is the most excellent. Is this interpretation correct? Answer: It is absolutely not.

Furthermore, those who conceive the thought of nirvana within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* yet seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land—does this not constitute the turning back of those with fixed natures?
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas know for themselves that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This is spoken in contrast to Bodhisattvas; it refers to how they originally resolved upon the Great Mind in the past and ultimately return to the Great Vehicle. It is not intended to manifest [the path] for the two vehicles.

Zhuokai asked: "Regarding the statement in this sutra that those of fixed nature all attain the One Vehicle, is this attainment realized in the present life, or is it the same as in the *Lotus Sutra*, where they attain it only in that [Pure] Land?
The answer is: Both meanings are applicable. If so, does it follow that there would be no one attaining it in the present life in the *Lotus Sutra*?
This requires a careful understanding of the intent of the scripture. The sutra says: "If there be bhikṣus who have truly attained arhatship, yet do not believe this... [and so forth].
It is impossible for this to be so; rather, it compels them to turn their minds toward awakening in the present life.

It is only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that those who turn their minds are pointed out as belonging to the future. If you understand this meaning, do not slander the Lotus Sūtra by claiming it is inferior to the present sūtra.

▲ Regarding the passage "The nature-awareness is wondrously luminous" (*xingju miaoming*) in the *Zhuxingfu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith), it says: "This is deluded awareness. It arises from the nature by taking luminosity as its object;

because it gives rise to awareness based on luminosity, it is called 'delusion. Deluded luminosity is called 'wondrous' [in this context]. Regarding the passage "The fundamental awareness is wondrously luminous" (*benjue mingmiao*) in the *Zizhong* (Zi Zhong’s Commentary), it says:

"Wondrous refers to the fundamental reality. The source is profound and still; its tranquil substance is free from delusion. It is wondrously pure and eternally as-it-is; therefore, it is called 'wondrously luminous.'"

"Nature-awareness that is wondrously luminous" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) while still enmeshed in defilements; because its fundamental nature is pure and is not stained by afflictions, it is called "nature-awareness.
"Fundamental awareness that is luminous and wondrous" refers to True Suchness beyond the enmeshment of defilements;

because one has awakened through non-discriminative wisdom to the exhaustion of beginningless delusive thoughts, it is called "ultimate awakening. Thus, initial awakening is identical to fundamental awareness; the awakening that realizes this fundamental [nature] is termed "awakening to the source."
It is the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Furthermore, the commentary on the subsequent section states in full: "Because the essence is itself the function. As the text below says:

"I, by means of wondrous clarity that is neither extinguished nor born, unite with the Tathāgata-garbha; and since the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, awakened clarity, therein one becomes the immeasurable," and so forth.
Because the function is itself the essence, the text below says: "Contemplating that the nature is originally true, it is solely wondrous..."

Question: Previously, when discussing space (*ākāśa*), it was stated that there is no karma or its fruit; yet here, when discussing karma and its fruit, why is space not mentioned? Answer: The previous treatise required the demonstration of space in order to reveal the nature of delusive appearances, for it is through delusion that space appears to exist as a basis. However, since this present discussion concerns the actual operation of karma and its results, there is no need to mention space. Furthermore, because space is devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, it does not participate in the causal process of karma and its retribution. Therefore, it is not discussed here. Moreover, space is merely a designation for the absence of obstruction; since it lacks the capacity to produce effects, it is not included among the factors of karma and its fruit. Finally, the previous discourse on space was intended to clarify the distinction between the real and the unreal, whereas the current discussion focuses on the actual functioning of karmic causality, which is why space is not explicitly named. This is the reason for the difference.

Answer: In the teaching of the Dharma, there are matters of sudden and gradual according to the capacities of the recipients; since this applies to both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it is likewise so for the precepts (*vinaya*).

Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* establishes a sudden prohibition for those with the capacities of the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Mahāyāna) vehicles, thereby permanently forbidding the consumption of meat. Therefore, having opened the three paths of purification, as the process of transformation nears its end, one gathers the gradual back into the sudden. Thus, all three sutras proclaim the cessation of meat-eating;

Regarding the four reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms]: first, because they are secret, as in the case of *dhāraṇī*;

The phrase "the sūtra has not yet reached nirvāṇa" refers to ultimate nirvāṇa, which is that realized by the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). The question, "By what gradual sequence does one obtain the vision of cultivation?
concerns the primary practice for entering the stages (*bhūmi*). According to the three kinds of gradual sequences explained below, the first step is to eliminate their auxiliary causes.

What is called the "five pungent roots" does not yet constitute the primary practice; rather, it refers to the second stage, which involves excising their fundamental nature—that is, the mind of lust.

For this reason, by cultivating *samādhi*, one can counteract present karmic activities and attain the third stage, even reaching the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, the second gradual stage is called "True Cultivation," which is the very designation for the practice itself; this should be understood.
Nirvana is like the destination reached; the various stages (*bhūmi*) are like the path traversed; and spiritual practice is like the steps taken upon it.
If these three factors are complete, then the purpose of the *Śūraṅgama* teaching is finally fulfilled. How magnificent! Such was Ānanda’s intention in making his request. II.

Reversing this non-awakening and understanding that, fundamentally, there is no arising is called "awakening," which is the designation for *bodhi*. This is established because of non-awakening. Due to delusion, there is arising, and with arising comes cessation.
To reverse this cycle of arising and cessation and reveal that which is neither arising nor ceasing is the designation for *nirvāṇa*.

It is established in contrast to arising and ceasing. Since arising and ceasing have ceased, there is nothing further upon which to rely; therefore, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the basis for both delusion and enlightenment, transforming this basis of delusion into a basis of enlightenment is called "transformation of the basis," and so forth.

Because there are eighteen hot hells, eighteen wheel-of-swords hells, and so forth up to eighty-four thousand hells, one knows that the distinctions among the characteristics of the hells are manifold.

This explanation refers to cases where one of the six faculties is predominant; however, this does not mean that the other faculties are not involved. Thus, it differs from what was stated in the preceding text.

The three individuals previously cited by Ānanda were questioned specifically regarding those who are most heavily burdened within the evil destinies. That the Buddha now speaks of them following the animal realm is intended to demonstrate that the three evil destinies share a common nature;
as clarified above, both ghosts and animals are all scorched by the fires of hellish karma.
Since even those such as Qianshengqiqu (乾出生其趣) and Baolianxiang (寶蓮香) could not escape this retribution, it was for this reason that he demonstrated it herein;

Regarding the third, which speaks of "awakening and perfect completion," it means severing the functions of sight and hearing so that one becomes like withered wood, and so forth (according to that commentary).
Question: What is meant by "corpse-liberation"? Answer: The *Zhen'gao* (True Declarations) of the Daoist school states: "The Way possesses both the Yin and the Yang. If one refines..."
When form and the Way unite and the respiration is purely yang, the physical body undergoes a gradual transformation and shedding.

As it sheds, it becomes increasingly subtle until the body enters the formless state. The skin shed during this transformation is exactly like the shell of a cicada; after the metamorphosis, because there are no bones or remains, even if one is buried in a tomb, only the sword, writing tablet, shoes, and staff remain.

This is the "Yang Passage" (yang-du). Now, as for the "Yin Passage" (yin-du): [...]* *Note: The source text contains a lacuna marked by "▲". The translation provided above reflects the available portion.*
Regarding the terrestrial immortals (*dixian*), their supernatural wisdom is well-documented;

the *Lengyan jing qiju chao* (Commentary on the Seven Destinies of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) quotes their texts extensively, as do the *Shengwu jing* and *Jiuzhen jing*, which clarify that the accounts of these immortals are largely hollow and extravagant—I dare not venture to accept such claims.

As for the claim of "pointing at stone to turn it into gold," I fear this interpretation does not equal that of Master Yuan. Why? Because even the transformation of hard metal and stone is merely a matter of ingesting [alchemical elixirs].

Regarding the excellence of these methods of nourishment: it is because all ten immortals achieved their realization by means of mental visualization (*saṃkalpa*) and the stabilization of the physical form.

If one speaks instead of pitying the poor or compassion for the suffering, these are merely external matters; how can they be called "stabilizing the form"? As for the statement that "this heaven is no different [from others]," Yuan’s commentary on the *Tianxing* (Heavenly Practice) explains:
"This heaven is not among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it is like Zhang Qian reaching the summit of Mount Kunlun and obtaining..."

Seeing the celestial palaces, one cannot yet suddenly transcend them. For now, following the ancient interpretation, this is a concluding passage from Gushan’s citation of Zhenji’s commentary on the "Ten Immortals," suggesting that the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Sections) is not entirely accurate.
Furthermore, Guyang, relying on Cui Xuanshan’s *Laiqing Ji*, states: "Laozi was the teacher of the thirteen sages; they cultivated their nature and attained immortality, each [in their own way]."

There are thirty-six methods of the "Self-Existent Dharma" (Zìyǒufǎ), which are sometimes arranged according to the Five Elements and the Six Jia stems, or involve practices such as ingesting elixirs to refine the bones and sinews, or even the removal of desire to preserve the spirit (*shén*).
Some of these thirty-six methods correspond quite closely with these [practices of the] Ten Immortals (*shíxiān*).
(From the *Cāowén*) Now, it is said that the words of Xuānshān were transmitted from the erroneous customs of the world, yet when Master Yuán cited them, they [turned out to be consistent].

The preceding words and meaning of Ge Hong are quite unlike [those of the Daoist tradition], which I find deeply startling. Examining Liu Xie’s *Miehuo lun* (Treatise on Extinguishing Delusions), it says:

"The Daoists establish their laws with three grades: the highest extols Laozi; the next describes the Immortals; and the lowest follows Zhang Ling. The *Taishang* (Supreme) is taken as the primary source.
Seeking the records of the Grand Historian (*Zhushi*), we find that his noble seclusion was truly that of a Great Sage; he authored books to discuss the Way, valuing..."
In the principle of non-action (*wuwei*), all returns to stillness and unity; the fundamental nature is empty and supple.

Yet, as the three periods of time are not recorded therein and the traces of wise deeds are unheard of, this is but an excellent book for guiding the secular world, not a sublime scripture for transcending it.
Thus, it is clear that Xuanshan [Sengrui] falsely attributed the Way of the Immortals to the Way of Laozi. Furthermore, Dao’an’s *Treatise on the Two Teachings* states: "The spirit ascends..."

The accounts of shedding feathers like a cicada, corpse-liberation, and the transformation of form are even more inconsistent with the fundamental principles established by Laozi and Zhuangzi in their teachings.

Yet, in the records of Master Lai (Lai Qing), it is said that some "wander the celestial mountains through the inhalation and exhalation of breath," while others "fly across the clouds in purity. Furthermore, there are records concerning the medicinal stones used in the tenth month;
these are greatly inconsistent [with the aforementioned principles]. One must ask: does the Way of the Immortals truly contain the principle of longevity and immortality? It would seem so.
As for why [Laozi] is ranked above [the Buddha], while Liu Xie suppresses him to the Middle Grade:
if a thing has fame but lacks substance, the gentleman does not accept it; what suppression could there be in that? Thus Mouzi said:

"The books of the immortals such as Wang Qiao and Chi Song, when heard, are grand and fill the ears, yet seeking their efficacy is like grasping at the wind or catching a shadow. He further said: "Yao and Shun..."
The Duke of Zhou and Confucius each could not live for more than a hundred years;
yet those of the degenerate age, deluded and ignorant, desire to ingest elixirs and abstain from grain in pursuit of infinite longevity. How lamentable!
Formerly, the eminent monk Tanluan sought the methods of the immortals to prolong his life, and thus traveled to the south to seek them from Tao [Hongjing].
While seeking them in his place of seclusion, he obtained ten scrolls of these books. Upon arriving in Luoyang, he met the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of China.
Sengluan asked, "Is there such a method for longevity and immortality within the Buddha-dharma? Bodhiruci spat on the ground and said, "What kind of talk is this?
This is not the mark of the Dharma. Where in this land is there a gate to birth without death? Thereupon, he burned the books.
If such books exist, is it not then false that the present sutras state, "By contemplating and solidifying the form, one’s lifespan shall reach ten million years"? Answer:

Although these books do not exist in this land, there may have been those who, having studied the four Vedas of the outsiders in the Western Heaven (India), cultivated various meditative concentrations and attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
For instance, the Rishi Kanakamuni, fearing death, went to the Heaven of Maheśvara and asked [various questions], as related in detail. It should be understood accordingly.
One should understand that the great illusionists mentioned in the preceding text, such as the sages Kapila and Śākalya, cannot be compared to the non-Buddhists of this world;
how much less so can they be compared to the ten sages of the present day? These ten sages all perfected their paths through the refinement of the mind;

Thus, the ten types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the ten objects of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Furthermore, regarding the eleven types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the eleven sense bases (*āyatana*)—the first ten are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the ten sense bases," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the base of mental objects" (*dharmāyatana*). Thus, the eleven types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the eleven sense bases. Furthermore, regarding the twelve types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*)—the first eleven are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the causal links," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the resultant link. Thus, the twelve types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the twelve links of dependent origination. Furthermore, regarding the thirteen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the thirteen abodes of beings (*sattvāvāsa*)—the first twelve are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the twelve abodes," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the non-abode. Thus, the thirteen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the thirteen abodes of beings. Furthermore, regarding the fourteen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the fourteen unanswerable questions (*avyākṛta-vastu*)—the first thirteen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the answerable questions," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the unanswerable questions. Thus, the fourteen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the fourteen unanswerable questions. Furthermore, regarding the fifteen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—the first fourteen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the preparatory path," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the path of seeing. Thus, the fifteen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the fifteen moments of the path of seeing. Furthermore, regarding the sixteen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths (*satya-ākāra*)—the first fifteen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the conventional truth," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the ultimate truth. Thus, the sixteen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, regarding the seventeen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the seventeen stages of the Bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*)—the first sixteen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the stages with outflows," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the stage without outflows. Thus, the seventeen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the seventeen stages of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, regarding the eighteen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)—the first seventeen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the seventeen elements," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the element of consciousness" (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Thus, the eighteen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the eighteen elements. Furthermore, regarding the nineteen types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the nineteen types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*)—the first eighteen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the eighteen types of mental engagement," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the mental engagement of equanimity" (*upekṣā-manasikāra*). Thus, the nineteen types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the nineteen types of mental engagement. Furthermore, regarding the twenty types of afflictions—namely, afflictions of the twenty types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—the first nineteen are subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the emptiness of phenomena," while the latter is subsumed under the category of "afflictions of the emptiness of the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Thus, the twenty types of afflictions are fully encompassed by the twenty types of emptiness. It is said that just as an echo arises from thought, there are cases in the world where conception occurs not through sexual union but through thought alone;

thus, it is highly verifiable that the physical body arises from thought. According to the *Baoshoushen ji* (Records of Searching for Spirits), during the end of the Han dynasty, the daughter of the Governor of Lingling fell in love with a clerk at the prefectural gate.
She then sent a maidservant to fetch the clerk, give him water, and have him drink it.

When she became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to a son who was able to walk, the Governor saw the rafters and took up the child in his arms amidst the crowd, ordering them to seek out the father.

The child climbed directly onto the clerk’s (shū-zo) lap; when the Governor pushed him away, he turned into water. The crowd was greatly astonished, and consequently, they betrothed their daughter to the clerk.
By this it is made clear that although there are differences between those born through sexual union and those not born through sexual union, there are none that do not [arise from causes].

This is entirely due to people’s perception of the account that the child transformed into water, which they deem strange and miraculous, while failing to consider that a hundred years in this world is likewise like this child.
To grasp a physical body and form a physical body—that body is also water;
once it dies and perishes, its decaying remains are still water. If the boy of Lingling were truly so startling, then everyone would be [startling].

How startling! Since that [other] is already deceptive, how could this not be deceptive? It arises from false conceptualization (vikalpa). How great is the Buddha’s teaching! II. From "That which is precisely this...

This refers to the stage where, according to the Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao), the coarse defilements fall away first. Now, by means of awakening, one eliminates them simultaneously.

As for whether one first perceives [the objects] and then contemplates (*si*), or first contemplates and then perceives, or whether both perception and contemplation are severed together: the response should contain two meanings.

Even if one first perceives and then contemplates, it is still called "simultaneous elimination," because these two delusions both pervade the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). One should know that this applies from the first faith (*prathama-śraddhā*) onward.

Simultaneously eliminating the delusions regarding principle within the five aggregates: from the second stage of faith through the seventh stage of faith, one simultaneously eliminates the delusions regarding phenomena within the five aggregates.

There is scriptural authority for the meaning that both *darśana-heya* (delusions abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned by cultivation) are severed together; as the *Yingluo benye jing* states:

What is called "a single thought" refers to the mind within a single *kṣaṇa*. Furthermore, "a single thought" refers to the initial and final moments of the mind remaining unmoved from the preceding state.

Because subsequent moments of mind are all similar, "one thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa) refers to non-thought. Karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty, and the myriad virtues are primordially complete;

this is an explanation based on principle (*li*), whereas the preceding was a discussion based on phenomena (*shi*). Since principle and phenomena are mutually integrated, you should skillfully harmonize them yourself.
Now, according to the *Ratnaketu-parivarta* (Renwang jing), there are ninety kṣaṇas within one thought-moment; thus we know that "one thought-moment" refers to an extremely brief duration of time.
If that is so, does the Buddha’s intention imply that the power of upholding the sutra is superior only for those whose preceding and succeeding thoughts remain steadfast from beginning to end?
Furthermore, if one explains this according to principle, it pertains to the meaning of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*) and not to the sense of benefiting others (*parārtha*) within this context.

How fortunate it is that even for a single moment of thought, the destruction of evil is thus; how much more so for a long duration, and how much more so for a lifetime! Since this is already the case, [the benefit] is all the more certain.
It is said that the speech of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is without falsehood and cannot be explained away by means of intentional terminology regarding different times.

Thus, the upholding of four lines of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is superior to giving away the entire bodies of three hundred koṭis of beings; the realization of half a verse of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* surpasses the attainment of the small fruits of the Śrāvakas by those who have transformed hundreds of koṭis of beings.
If this is so when comparing them in detail, how much more so would it be for the complete [teachings]? Furthermore, if even these verses and phrases are thus, how much more so the entirety?

Having completed the purification of my faculties and the fulfillment of my duties, I am filled with joy. This commentary on the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* encompasses the three teachings;
now, only the coarse and the subtle within the Perfect and Sudden teaching can be discerned.

I am concerned that my previous explanations of the textual sections remain sparse and fear that the path of meaning for future generations may still be obstructed; therefore, I wish to provide further assistance by composing this record.

It was written in the fourth year of the Qingli era (1048) while I was fulfilling an invitation to reside at the Western Mountain Hermitage (Lanruo). Having first lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I lectured on this same scripture again in the fifth year.
Since the location is secluded amidst forests and springs, there is much leisure time for the incense and lamps; it was for this reason that I took up my pen.
To fulfill my former aspiration, I have recorded these matters totaling several tens of thousands of words, divided into five fascicles.
I hope that both the recorder and the listener will not forget this path of perfect penetration and essential brevity; therefore, it is titled *Xunwen* (Perfuming the Hearing).
